Mr. JOSEPH ARCHAMBAULT (Cham-bly and Vercheres) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 105 to amend the Act to revive and amend the Naturalization Act, 1914.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the Bill is to remedy a grave injustice, now existing I believe through an oversight in regard to subjects of the Allied countries who went overseas and fought in the Allied armies. The Naturalization Act of 1914 requires of an alien a residence of five years, within the last eight years, in His Majesty's Dominions, the last year's residence preceding the application for naturalization having been in Canada. At the outbreak of the war, in order not to embarrass aliens who had enlisted in the Crown forces, the law was amended in such a way as to provide that the time passed in such forces should count as residence in Canada for the purposes of naturalization. Paragraph 6 of subsection 2, of section 3 of the Act, to revive and amend the Naturalization Act of 1914, reads as follows:
For the purposes of this section a period spent in the service of the Crown may, if the Secretary of State of Canada thinks fit, be treated as equivalent to a period of residence in Canada.
The service of the subjects of Allied countries in the armies of the Allies has evidently been overlooked, for they do not benefit by this clause, and the consequence is that the Belgian, or the Frenchman, or the Italian who resided in Canada before the war and who had to join the forces of Belgium, or France, or Italy, does not benefit by that service. He has to reside, after

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
coming back to Canada, another five years, or possibly ten years, according to another amendment of last year, to the Naturalization Act. The time he spent in Canada before the war, or the time in which he was in the service of any Allied army, does not count. Furthermore, this fact does not enable the alien who served in His Majesty's Allied armies to obtain his patent for homestead, because to do so he must be a British subject. A case has been brought to my notice of a Belgian who came to Canada in 1910. He resided in this country four years, and when the war broke out joined the Belgian army, and when he came back in 1919 he had to start all over again. He had to begin the period of five years' residence-and possibly, because of the amendment to which I have referred, it may be ten years-before he can obtain his naturalization papers and have the right to apply for patent for homestead. The object of my Bill is to remedy this situation by adding after the words "Crown Forces" in paragraph 6, the words "or in His Majesty's Allied armies." I think this would remedy a grave injustice which, in my opinion, is just the result of oversight on the pa-rt of the Government.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: topic

speechtext:
On the Orders of the Day:
Mt.' ERNEST LAPOINTE (Quebec East) :	Before the Orders of the Day are
called I desire to rise to a question of privilege in regard to a statement published in the press which affects very seriously and is a reflection upon many members of this House, including myself. In both the Globe and the Mail and Empire of Wednesday, April 20, apears a report of a meeting held in Toronto which was addressed by a gentleman styled in the report "A. L. Davidson, M.P., for Digby and Antigonish" and who is reported as having made the following statement concerning the leader of the Opposition and his selection as leader of the Liberal party: "The Rockefeller interests of the United States thought it would be a good idea if they could have one of their former employees leader of a nation party in Canada, and they were willing to spend a little money to attain that end," said Mr. Davidson. Down in Quebec there were a number of young men who were willing to go to the Convention and support Mr. King if somebody else paid the expenses.
Mr. Speaker, the statement made there constitutes a foul, mean, despicable slander.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have grave doubt
whether it is competent for the hon. member to rise to a question of privilege with respect to a matter that does not affect himself personally. If the hon. gentleman feels himself aggrieved there is a well-known constitutional method open to him to follow. I hope that the hon. member will not continue in the manner in which he has just expressed himself.

I need not remind
you, Mr. Speaker, that I was one of those at the convention referred to. I was a member of this House at the time and further I was one of "the young men" alluded to.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The point I had reference to was this: if there is any question
of privilege with respect to a matter which very seriously reflects on an hon. member of this House, there is a well recognized method of procedure, and I do not think it would be competent for the hon. gentleman to deal with such a matter as this on the Orders of the Day.

The hon. gentleman
who is reported to have made the statement is here and he has the opportunity to say now whether he made the statement or not.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It would be neither
competent nor desirable to put any hon. member of this House on his trial on the Orders of the Day. I think the good sense of the House will realize that there is a well-recognized method of procedure if the hon. member desires to take further action.
I must bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker, but I think the proceeding of which I complain shows to what tactics the hon. gentleman in question will resort.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (leader of the Opposition) :
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
This is a matter which reflects upon me personally and therefore I trust, Mr. Speaker, I shall be granted the opportunity of making a statement at the present moment. If it is permissible to say that the statement which has just been quoted, made by a member of this House outside the precincts of Parliament was made in the knowledge that it was untrue and false, I would say that the hon. gentleman who made the statement made it knowing that it was false and untrue. It is an absolutely false and untrue statement. I have never, at any time in my life, been in the employ of the so-called Rockefeller interests. I was, as the hon. members of this House know, engaged for a time in research work for the Rockefeller Foundation, a philanthropic corporation which has nothing whatever to do with the Rockefeller business interests one way or the other. What I did for the Rockefeller Foundation was research work in connection with problems of industry of public interest and the results of which have found a place in a book published by me entitled "Industry and Humanity," which is known, I think, to hon. members of this House and to the country. That is the only connection I have had at any time with any institution bearing the name of Rockefeller. I say that when any hon. member of this House, or any person in Canada, makes a statement such as this



one which appeared in the Toronto Globe and other papers, he makes it for a malicious and wrongful purpose well knowing it to be false and untrue.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think it is perfectly competent for the hon. leader of the Opposition to say that a statement made with respect to him, and which is a matter peculiarly within his own knowledge, is untrue, but I do not think the hon. gentleman is in order in asserting that another hon. gentleman has made a statement which is deliberately false and untrue.
He knows it is untrue.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: For the hon. the leader of the Opposition to make such a statement as the one referred to is going far beyond the amenities of debate, and he would be well advised to withdraw that statement.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I said what I believed, that is all.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. leader of the Opposition is not setting a good example when, in reference to a newspaper report of an hon. member's speech, he makes the statement that that hon. member deliberately stated something false and untrue. I think that remark the hon. leader of the Opposition should withdraw. It is, of course, perfectly competent for him to say that a given statement made with respect to him, and as to which he has special, and peculiar knowledge, is false.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I stated from my place in this House some time ago in the hearing of all hon. members of this House what my connection with the Rockefeller Foundation was. My statement appears in Hansard, the hon. gentleman in question heard it, and he knows its precise terms. I say, therefore, that it was impossible for him to go to Toronto, or anywhere else, and make the statement Which he did without knowing he was stating something that was not true.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The newspaper report in question may be absolutely untrue, and I repeat it is not competent to conduct the trial of a matter of this kind on the Orders of the Day, but it is perfectly proper for the hon. member to say that a certain statement with respect to a matter which is peculiarly within his own knowledge is false and untrue. To say, however, that a certain hon. member of this House made

a statement knowing it to be false and untrue is certainly not in accordance with the amenities of debate or parliamentary decorum.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If the statement that appeared in the press was not a correct statement of what my hon. friend said then, of course, I bow to your ruling. But if it is a correct statement of what he said, I have not one word to retract.

Mr. Speaker, I would
say further, that if I were allowed I would characterize this statement as being cowardly.

stagedirection
speechtext: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. 80, respecting the Grand Trunk Arbitration.

Mr. Speaker, before this Bill receives second reading I think we should have some further information from the Government in regard to it. About two weeks ago the Prime Minister laid on the table of the House the correspondence up to April 3 relating to the failure to complete the arbitration proceedings, but there must surely have been some further correspondence culminating in this Bill, otherwise this legislation would not now be engaging our attention.
I took occasion on April 13 to ask the Prime Minister if in his opinion, or in the opinion of the Government, the Canadian people were released from the agreement of March 8, 1920, by reason of the failure to complete the arbitration proceedings, but he did not see fit to give me an answer. I think that before this Bill is proceeded with the people and hon. members should have an answer from the Prime Minister as to just where we stand with regard to this arbitration. It is rumoured that if we drop the proceedings now we will be bound by the agreement guaranteeing the interest on certain debenture stock. On the other hand, it may be argued that if the agreement of 1920 is dropped in this particular it will be dropped in its entirety and that we shall be back to where we were before that agreement was entered into.
155i
That Bill was brought in originally in the last days of the session of 1919, and it was rushed through the House. Then again in the session of 1920 another enabling Bill was brought down, and that also was rushed through the House. Now we find the muddle has been continued, and it is necessary to come to this House with further legislation. But no explanation is given of why this Bill should be gone on with. There is an item in the Estimates of $89,000,000, presumably to be paid to the Grand Trunk stockholders. I am sure the people are interested in knowing just where we stand in regard to this Grand Trunk deal, and I think they and the members of this House should be enlightened on the subject. If we are released from the agreement by the Grand Trunk people failng to complete their case before the arbitrators within the time specified, then it would seem to me that the whole question is open for further negotiation, if it is desired to reopen it. I would like to know from the Prime Minister if it is the opinion of the Government that the responsibility of Canada ceased when the Grand Trunk directors failed to comply with the terms of the agreement in respect to getting their case before the arbitration board. If he feels that the Government is in honour bound to continue the arbitration, he would of course continue it under the original agreement of March, 1920. If that is not the case, the question should be debated on its merits as to whether we want to involve this country any further in railway transactions about which, apparently, we know very little-but we do know we will be called upon this year to pay some $89,000,000 in respect to this transaction on top of other financing that has been done in guaranteeing certain bonds of the Grand Trunk railway.
I would like to know if the Prime Minister thinks Canada can honourably wash her hands of the whole transaction, or if we are in honour bound to continue the arbitration. If we are, we should have an explanation from the Prime Minister, or the minister in charge of the matter, as to just what is the position of the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway. I quite agreed with the Prime Minister the other day when he said that they really had no grievance against the Canadian people. I would go further and say that if there is any grievance it is on the part of the Canadian people. The Canadian people have a grievance in that they have

been called upon to arbitrate and pay for a stock that is absolutely worthless. The proper procedure would have been to let the Grand Trunk company finance itself, but the Government saw fit to relieve the company from that obligation. We would like to know just what position we stand in now in consequence of that action by the Government. I might go further and say that the stock which is being arbitrated to-day is the minority stock, not the stock of the owners who agreed with the Government to arbitrate. What position are the minority and the majority shareholders in to-day? Are we still negotiating with the majority shareholders? I think this has been a stock-jobbing proposition from the start. I do not think any great responsibility can be laid on the Canadian people, but I do believe the Government is responsible for entering into these negotiations in the first place. I believe that Mr. Smithers is part of that stock-jobbing proposition. He was quite willing to sell out his interest. He was quite willing to co-operate with the Government in getting the majority stock vote to put through this transaction but he threw the minority shareholders out. Well, I would like to know just what position these people arb in to-day and whether we have any further responsibility in connection with this matter. I think we should have some additional information before we proceed with the second reading of the Bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton and Victoria) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think
we should have some explanation from the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) or from some other member of the Government- the Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid), for instance-with regard to the purpose and effect of this Bill. I say this now because when the Bill gets into copimittee we will be told that we have accepted the principle of the Bill and may not attack it except in matters of detail.
It is well known to the Prime Minister, who was in charge of the proposal in its early stages, that I was opposed to it. I was always opposed to the taking over of this railway and I now have more reasons than ever to be opposed to it. We were told by the Government, particularly by the Prime Minister, who was the Minister of the Interior I believe, that it was necessary to take over this system in order to make the rest of the Government-owned railways a paying proposition. If that could be brought about it would, be a very
fMr. Cahill.1
desirable thing, but we on this side could not see any evidence that that result would follow. Early this session the Minister of Railways announced a deficit for part of the year on operations alone of something like $25,000,000 in respect of the Grand Trunk, the road that was going to make us happy and wealthy. We are now so accustomed to talking in millions and billions that perhaps we do not realize what these large amounts mean. After less than an year's experience we find that we are something like $100,000,000 behind on the whole railway transaction, of which twenty-five millions is deficit in operation of the road which was supposed to be taken over as a source of income. In view of that experience I would be glad to help, if I could, in getting clear of this road altogether and letting it stay with the people who own it. I do not remember very clearly what the terms of the agreement were. The whole transaction was put through entirely against my judgment in the matter and the judgment of the party to which I belong, and so far as details are concerned I must confess that I have not been following the agreement very closely. But if there is any honourable way by which, even at this stage, we can do so, I would suggest that we say to the Grand Trunk people:	Keep
your railway; we have suffered loss in the transaction, but if you think we have been treating you unfairly, take your property back, utilize it as best you can, and let us go our way and take care of the railway properties that we already have. That, Sir, would be my position in connection with this road if it is a position that could honourably be taken.
The purpose of this legislation would seem to be to take charge of the property of the Grand Trunk, whether or not the owners are willing to give it up-in fact, to expropriate it, and take the consequences whatever they may be in a financial sense. I wish to point out that I have grave doubts as to the power of this Parliament to legislate in connection, with the very large section of this railway which is in the United States. I do not, think we have any power to enact legislation ^putting under the control of the Government property which is in a foreign country. I do not wish to elaborate the point, but I do submit that we are legislating against property that is not in Canada and against persons who are not Canadians and not living on Canadian territory. This we cannot properly do. And the same applies to stocks owned by persons beyond the jurisdiction of this

Parliament-residents of England, Scotland, Ireland and other countries than Canada. Those persons may have in their possession stocks affected by this agreement -stocks perhaps deposited with banks or put up as security or held by third parties.
I do not think we can legislate in such a way as to force whoever may be holding these stocks to deliver them up. I am stating these things in a general way, to indicate clearly what my own views are with regard to any legislation which we may pass here for the purpose of acquiring a property beyond the jurisdiction of the Canadian Parliament. This phase of the question was evidently had in mind by the Government during last session, for the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) had a notice on the Order Paper last year the purpose of which was to give to this Parliament extra-territorial jurisdiction. It was evidently the feeling or the judgment of the Government at that time that it was necessary to extend the power of Parliament in that way in order to have this jurisdiction. That resolution, if I remember correctly, was not dealt with last session; no legislation of the kind was passed. If that legislation was necessary last year in order to complete the jurisdiction, it is still necessary, and if it can be brought about, we should have it as a preliminary step to passing legislation as far-reaching as this legislation is intended to be.
I do not propose to detain the House any longer. All I say is this, that the taking over of the Grand Trunk appears to me now as it always has done, a poor transaction, a poor piece of business, something for which we are undertaking to pay huge amounts of money and getting property which is not worth the money. The way to look upon these things is:	What
is the income?-what is the result? The money may he properly invested in the railways, hotels, bridges, coal mines and all that other property which is owned by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, but what is the good of all that unless it is productive? We in this country want to have property that will pay its way and leave some balance for betterments. If the whole transaction would show or indicate in any way that it is going to pay its way, that the people of Canada will not be called upon to put their hands in their pockets to back up this enterprise, all well and good; but there are no such indications to-day. And as I said before, if there is any way of getting clear of this and leaving the property with the people who own it, and getting along ourselves with the very disagreeable burden of railways which we-have apart from this and which we must deal with, I would feel very happy. I believe this Grand Trunk railway which we are talking about taking over is in a starved and wrecked condition. My belief is that the Grand Trunk Railway Company has been for years contemplating this sale and transfer, and the moneys which should have gone into the road and which would have kept it in condition, have been milked out of it in profits to the shareholders and the paying of dividends, in the hope that what has happened would happen and that we would be called upon to make up the deficiency. The Drayton-Acworth report, which we used to read so often in connection with the railway problems of this country, stated that about $50,000,000 would be necessary to bring this road up to a proper standard. That was some four or five years ago. I venture to think that not only is that condition present still, but it is two-fold what it was then or more than that; that to-day, when we are taking over this road, two or three hundred millions of money will be necessary to put it into shape, and after we have put it into shape, we shall likely have the experience which we are having now of having deficits running into twenty-five or thirty millions of money from year to year on the Grand Trunk alone. We have had experiences enough in the past with ventures of this kind to teach us to keep clear of any further such enterprises'if we can possibly do so. I would urge upon the Prime Minister and the Government to give serious consideration to that phase of the subject.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must direct the attention of the House to the fact that if the Prime Minister exercises his right to reply, the debate will be closed. Therefore, if any other hon. gentleman desire's to speak on this question, he should do so now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I did not address the House on the moving of the second reading, for the very obvious reason that on the introduction of the Bill I had given a statement that would ordinarily be made on a second reading. That was done then in order that hon. members would have, as early as possible in the debate, the Gov-

ernment's position and the reasons for it.
In the two speeches which have been delivered, there have been addressed to me certain questions which I am asked to answer, in relation to the measure itself. I shall endeavour to do so. I do not need to reiterate the reasons for.the Bill. The agreement that was entered into, by authority of Parliament on our part, by authority of the shareholders on the part of the Grand Trunk, provided for an arbitration. It provided that the arbitration should be completed and the award made within nine months from the appointment of the arbitrators. It stated that that time might be extended by approval-I think the word used is "approval"-of the Governor in Council; in any case it could only be extended by approval of the Governor in Council. That period expired on the 9th day of April., The Governor in Council had declined, and did decline to the last, to approve an extension. Consequently, the arbitration lapsed. That phase of the agreement falls and can only be revived, so far as we are concerned, by Parliament; the Governor in Council has no power to revive it. The purpose of the Bill is to revive it, and having revived it, to place the parties in the position to continue in which they were before; but the Bill provides that the Governor in Council can only revive the arbitration if certain stipulated terms are agreed to by the Grand Trunk. That, very briefly, is the purpose of the Bill. Of course, I know it will be my duty to give in committee any details that may reasonably be asked for.
Is action by the Governor in Council necessary, after the passing of the Bill, to revive proceedings?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is, in this sense, that the Bill authorizes an agreement to be made by the Governor in Council. Consequently, the Governor in Council must act to make the agreement. That is all that is necessary. The hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) asked if there was any further correspondence. The only further correspondence-and there is some significance to this fact-is one letter received from Messrs Kelley and Phippen, written on behalf of the Grand Trunk, and my acknowledgement of their letter. Their letter was received the very day that the correspondence was laid on the table; my reply followed a day or two afterward, simply acknowledging the letter. No communication of any kind whatsoever has passed between us since. I will ask for that (Mr. Meighen.]
letter and my reply immediately, and I will lay them upon the Table when we are in committee. The letter consisted simply of a legal argument presented by Messrs. Kelley and Phippen; something to the effect that they had a right to the extension and that they could not hand over possession; also stating their opinion of what the obligations of the Government were. I felt that the whole matter that they urged in the letter had been covered sufficiently in previous correspondence, and that nothing was to be gained by continuing the correspondence.
What was the date of that letter?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It was the day that I laid the correspondence on the table. I will have it in a moment. There has been no correspondence since that I am aware of. The hon. member (Mr. Cahill) wants me to state the legal position as to the contract.
Do I understand my right hon. friend to say there was no correspondence beyond that to be brought down?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That and the acknowledgment. There was other correspondence on other phases, I think, before, but I brought down all the correspondence relating to the extension.
There is nothing later?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Except the letter I
have referred to, and my acknowledgment of it. That will be brought down.
I have just explained that there was a letter that arrived that day just a few minutes before I laid the correspondence on the Table. I acknowledged that a day or two afterwards. These two letters will be brought down when we are in committee.
Could they not have been brought down before now?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
They could, but I do not think it would have been of any advantage. The matter was covered in previous correspondence.
Now as to the legal position. It is a pretty general question to ask what are the rights of each party in respect of a contract of the extent and importance of this one and of its necessary complexity. Even if it were my peculiar duty, I would rather not answer without very, very careful inquiry indeed, and say just what I thought the rights of each were. Many of my hon.

friends opposite are lawyers; I was going to say, some of them are good lawyers; for the present I will say all of them are good lawyers. They can read the contract. It is our duty to state the facts, and they can come to their own conclusions. Where there may be any doubt I would be prepared to state it, if it would help put at all on any particular point, but it would clearly not be in the public interest that we should here in this committee or in this House make anything in the way of concession to the Grand Trunk by the way of admission of a position where there may be any doubt at all. That would appear to me to be a very wrong course in the public interest. This however, is clear. There is now no arbitration, and it can be revived in this way and in this way only. What the hon. member refers to is this: what is the obligation of the country in respect of the debenture and guaranteed stock. There may be doubt as to that but this I will say. This Government always has been, and is now, ready to take the Grand Trunk system and not request that it get it at a bigger sacrifice than the price of the underlying securities. We have always taken that position. We take it to-day; but if we attempt to take the Grand Trunk by force, to exercise the power of government to take it, or exercise our legislative jurisdiction to do so, whatever that may be, we should, I submit, have first armed ourselves by being able to show that we have 4 p.m. resorted to every possible defensible means to treat the holders of the other securities in absolute fairness. We consider this Bill one step in the way of arming ourselves with the proof that we did seek to do justice in this matter to those men, and not to be driven arbitrarily to assert the powers of government to extinguish those shares. I am sure that no one who has the real good of his country at heart, and values its reputation, would seek to exercise the powers of government before he knew for certain that he had exhausted other means, and put himself in a position to say that there was no just cause for any complaint.
The hon. member appeared to be under the impression that the Government had in some way relieved the Grand Trunk of the obligation to finance the system. That was not done. It may be that some of the correspondence would indicate such a feeling on the part of the Grand Trunk directors and shareholders. I do not know how that feeling arose; I do not know on what they
base that feeling, if, indeed, they have such an opinion.
They did set it up.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
They did at least
obliquely set it up. The agreement does not relieve them of any obligation to finance their system, not in any way whatever; that obligation still remains on them. Indeed, the Grand Trunk Pacific as yet is obliged legally to operate the Transcontinental. They were not able to do it, and we had to do it or see the thing crash. The same is true in relation to the Grand Trunk. They were obliged to finance their road, and are still obliged under the agreement to do it. They were not able to do it, and the country had to come to their rescue or see the thing dissipate, and take the consequences of that dissipation. That is the only sense in which they have been relieved. They are bound, as far as obligation goes, to finance the system just the same as before.
I have sought to answer questions put forward by hon. members. I do not know of anything in the way of question that was put in the very fair speech that was addressed to us by the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie). He does, of course, take the ground that we should not have reached out and acquired the road. I am afraid he has not quite apprehended the pyschology of the Administration in this regard. We were not in the reaching-out business; we were simply endeavouring to find the least unfortunate solution of a very grave and complex difficulty into which this country by a course of policy had come. We chose this as calculated best to meet the situation that confronted us; that is all. We were not seeking it; we only got to it by a process of eliminating others that seemed to us to be worse.

What position do the
Grand Trunk people take now with regard to the arbitration? Would they be satisfied to let the arbitration drop now?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not know, but if
this Bill passes, we will have to know, and know pretty soon.

I have not the agreement before me, but my recollection is that it contained a provision to the effect that the period of arbitration could be extended by the Government by Order in Council. If that is so, I think it is rather at variance with the statement made by my right hon.

friend a moment ago, that this legislation is necessary to extend the arbitration. I would like some information upon this.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Government had
power to extend, but no power to revive. You can only extend while the time continues. We could have extended the arbitration past the ninth of the month, if we had acted on or before the ninth, but once it had fallen, then we were of the opinion that we had no power to revive it, that only Parliament had the power to re-establish the arbitration after it had lapsed. We could have extended it prior to the ninth.
Am I in order in asking another question?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have no objection, if the Prime Minister desires to answer. I hope, however, we shall not get to the position where questions will be submitted as if we were in Committee of the Whole. The debate has been closed by the Prime Minister.

I think my point will
assist in determining the value of the principle of the Bill. I would like to ask my right hon. friend why the Government did not take action to extend the arbitration before its expiration on the ninth.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Because, as the correspondence shows, we offered to do so on certain terms, with which the Grand Trunk did not comply. The Grand Trunk not having complied with the conditions that were laid down, the conditions upon which we would have extended the arbitration, we stood by our position, and the arbitration lapsed.
Was the promise of a renewal of the arbitration by Order in Council conditional?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There was no promise of renewal at all. It was quite in our hands to renew or not to renew. Under the circumstances we felt that there should be these conditions, which they did not live up to.
While the session is on I prefer an Act of Parliament to an Order in Council. I thought it was not conditional.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We did not have to extend at all.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What were the terms on which the Government was prepared to continue the arbitration?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They are set out very clearly in the correspondence that was brought down the other day. There has been nothing since to alter them in the slightest degree. In a word it was: Give us possession of the road, and then we will extend.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1.-Governor in Council may extend time for arbitrators' award.

Will the Government
now give the correspondence which the Prime Minister has mentioned?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have sent for it; it
will-be here in a moment.

In the preamble, reference is made to section 8 of the Grand Trunk Railway Act of 1920, which reads as follows:
The award shall be made by the arbitrators, or a majority of them, within nine months from the appointment of the arbitrators, or within such further time as the Governor In Council may approve. The unanimous award of the arbitrators shall be final, but should the award not be unanimous, and should notice of appeal be given by either party to the other within thirty days after the making of the award, an appeal therefrom, upon any question of law, shall lie to the Supreme Court of Canada and or to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, if leave be granted by the said committee.
Is it intended to include a similar clause in the new agreement to be made?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
A subsequent section
of this Bill says, in effect, that the new agreement shall achieve the end set out here, and if it does, then it revives the arbitration, with the same rights to either party as the old agreement provided.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will the new agreement be submitted to Parliament for ratification?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is now being submitted to Parliament for ratification. The new agreement will provide certain things in accordance with this Bill. If Parliament so decides, these things, it can provide or if it desires other things, it can provide them; Parliament has full power-of course, Parliament takes the consequences of any legislation it does pass. We think that this is fair and just, and we ask Parliament to confirm us in that position. When that is done, and we say to the Grand Trunk "This is what we are ready to do" and they agree to it, we could not, after that, have any power to back out.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Did the old
agreement provide certain consequences if certain clauses were not complied with, and particularly this clause with regard to the arbitration proceedings being completed within a given time?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There was provision
that they should be completed within a certain time, which time could be extended if we saw fit. If they were not completed, then, of course, the Grand Trunk had to take the consequences of whatever Parliament might see fit to do under the circumstances.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What does
the Prime Minister think now are the legal consequences of the arbitration proceedings not having been completed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: One consequence is that if our proposals are supported by this House we shall have our property in the real sense, in the way we should have it. That is one consequence, and it is a consequence which the directors deem it of the utmost importance to them shall not ensue. The great difficulty in coming to the agreement before was in regard to this very question, and it was finally settled by a compromise with the committee of management. The question having been so settled, we insisted that there should be no delay beyond the nine months provided in the agreement. Had the Grand Trunk proceeded with the despatch which we though it should have shown, I would have thought it our duty to extend the time until the arbitration could be finished, and leave it in possession. in the meantime. But it did not proceed as rapidly as it should have done, and certainly was" not able to finance its business; so we take the position that it should abide by the consequences and give up the system at once.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: As in the case of all agreements, made as a result of legislation, there are certain legal consequences which can be determined in the courts as a matter of right, and which will leave beyond question and dispute any possibility of the parties being in any way imposed upon through additional legislation. Why is it necessary to come to Parliament for legislation now, if the Government is prepared, as the Grand Trunk must be, to take the legal consequences of its own agreement?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The legal consequences in that respect would be-I do not know
whether you could call them legal consequences or not, but the practical consequences would be-that the Grand Trunk would stay there in possession of the road under the same obligation to run it that it always had, but not able to discharge that obligation. Then this Government would be in the position of having to find some means to run the system, and while we were trying to do that possibly another section of the system owned by a subsidiary company would be in liquidation and that section, possibly would be alienated. That is one of the practical consequences that might ensue. We do not want that practical con-sequnece to ensue if we can reasonably avoid it. By this mode we seek reasonably to avoid it; it may have to ensue anyway.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Why should this road be treated differently from any other road, for example roads in the United States which, for obvious reasons, have had to go into liquidation? Let the Government acquire it then if it wishes to do so, or let other parties acquire it. Why should this road be dealt with otherwise than has been customary with regard to roads that have used any amount of public funds to no advantage?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Of course, in. the
growth of the railway industry, the roads naturally started as small, railways, and with the evolution of capitalism, as the hon. member knows better than I, the tendency has been towards larger and larger units, until we reached, in Canada, say, three very great systems. In the United States they have not concentered as they have in this country'; they have not had as great railway systems or as costly. But while their roads were allowed to go into liquidation, they were isolated and comparatively small railways as compared with the whole United States transport system, and there were not the consequences to be anticipated to the country by permitting liquidation. The very size of the system, the length of its history, the tremendous amount of capital, of labour, and of investment involved-all these things add to the magnitude of the catastrophe in the event of liquidation, not to the shareholders alone, but to all concerned including Canada. But there are special reasons here. Portions of the system-and some of them vital portions if the system is to serve its purpose for this country-are in the United States.
And you seek to acquire them?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What we seek to acquire is the stock that represents them. We feel that we can do that-in fact there is no question at all in the minds of our legal advisers but that we can.	.
Owned mostly in the British Isles?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is, as far as I know, in British hands, that is to say, it is owned there, but it is Canadian stock-it is a Canadian company although it is owned in the United Kingdom. The purpose of this Bill is to acquire it, and then we hold the system intact and keep it intact. Whether it can be held intact, or whether it is to slide down into liquidation or not, may be a grave question. We may have to consider that if this proposal is not accepted.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does not my right hon. friend's argument imply that, no matter what the cost, in order to save it and prevent any possibility of the road going into liquidation, we must continue to introduce new legislation and expend additional public funds?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We will certainly have to expend funds if it goes into liquidation, but we want to avoid that. I do not say we should not do anything at all to prevent it-I say we must be very careful that we do everything reasonable to prevent it. I say that if the time ever comes when the liquidation of the Grand Trunk system is upon us, the people of this country will hold us very strictly answerable that we have done everything that was reasonable and fair that we could be called upon to do to avoid the catastrophe that would ensue. They would hold us strictly accountable for that, and it is in order to answer that accountability that the Government of the day has decided to take this step as one means to avoid it if it can be avoided. What, in effect, does it mean? It simply means "You can^ have the intent of the old agreement-you can have that
but you can have it only on giving us possession. And the reason we insist on possession is this: the way things are going you have no right to remain in possession with our Government supporting the road out of the money of the people of Canada. You have no right to keep away from us any longer the

advantages we sought when the Grand Trunk was acquired." It was not all advantage, there were a lot of disadvantages, but there were certain advantages-the union of the two systems, the working together of the Grand Trunk and the national system, the economies that could be effected only by the amalgamation of each of the systems, and which would be still greater by the amalgamation of the whole. We say, "You have no right to deny them to this country any longer when you are asking us to advance $95,000,000 to run your system." And especially we felt that we had to take that position because the company was laying the ground for an appeal. The Board of Arbitration held that they would not admit evidence of the reproduction cost of the enterprise and taking exception to that ruling the company were preparing for an appeal. Well, the time expired, and if it was extended say three months, after that they might appeal, staying in possession all the while and calling for funds to run the system or let it go into liquidation. Under those circumstances we felt we were justified in saying " You are not through with your arbitration. The power to extend is ours and ours alone, but before we extend we ask you to hand it over." That in so many words is the whole purpose of this Bill.

It is
not very clear to me that it is an advantage to have possession of the road at the present junction. As I understand it, there is a large deficit day by day in the running of the road. My right hon. friend has mentioned the sum of $25,000,000 a year. That, roughly speaking, is $500,000 a week. The road is going behind. As I understand the present situation the Grand Trunk is liable for that loss; not the Government, but the Grand Trunk is liable for the deficit up to the time that we take it over. Now we will not be in a very good position if we forcibly take the road from the Grand Trunk and deprive them of any interference on the directorate. We are dismissing their directors, we are taking the road from them forcibly, and when it comes to settle up the question of a deficit that is incurred during the time the arbitration is proceeding, it will not be very easy for us to impose that liability upon the Grand Trunk on account of the fact that we have assumed the liabilities ourselves and the full responsibility of running the road.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think my hon. friend quite grasps the legal position. In

the first place there is no deficit, I am safe in saying, on the Grand Trunk in operation. There is under recent condi tions a deficit when you add together operation costs and fixed charges. We have been called on to finance that. We have been called upon not because the Grand Trunk was not liable-the Grand Trunk is liable-but because the Grand Trunk could not get the money; that is all. There is no difference in that respect before and after acquiring possession: we are the equitable owners of the system to-day. We are the equitable owners of the system under an agreement to purchase. Now all that was withheld was this: in the case of the Canadian Northern acquisition we got possession and went right in. In this case they hold out and take the ground that if we insist on possession at once upon acquisition, and previous to the termination of the arbitration, they would be kept out from access to evidence, that they said was essential, because the fullest access, they said, was needed by them to prove their case before the Board of Arbitration especially as the shareholders were a long distance away-over in England. It seemed they would hold the view very strongly that we had taken their road and shut the doors on them and not allowed them to go in so that they had the same power of direction as before, and they would say: " We put hundreds of millions into this Canadian venture; we have served your people for fifty years; and now you come, and, because we are in difficulties at this time,"-due to causes that they would like to wash their hands of it if they could-"you arrange an arbitration, drag it upon us, and shut the doors and exclude us from our own offices."
* Well, that never had as much force in my mind as it had in theirs. But we finally compromised on the plan of a committee of management. That gave a very, very qualified right of uniting the systems, and running them as one-in fact, we could not run them as one at all. And now we say to the Grand Trunk company: "You have had sufficient time to get your evidence and you have no doubt got it; you have no longer a right to remain in possession and operate a system that you do not really own; you have no right to say to us that this system has to be operated separately from the Canadian National system. We are willing to pay whatever the arbitrators find is coming to you; and, consequently, it is time for you to release the possession of that property."

Is the Grand Trunk
system at present meeting its operating expenses, and has it done so for the past year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Oh yes, and more; but not its fixed charges.
I understand that.
Has the right hon. gentleman received the additional letter which he referred to?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I have the letter.

What great harm does the Prime Minister think might come to Canada in the event of a receivership of the Grand Trunk railway system? If the Grand Trunk railway went into the hands of a receiver, he would issue receivership certificates, which would be a first security on the whole property, and the road would continue to be operated as it is now. The people who put their money into the company would lose some of it, but that is not any concern of ours; if these people made an investment which is not profitable to-day, it is not the business of Canada to take care of them. We have all made unprofitable investments, but we are not coming to the Government to help us. But I cannot see any force in the argument of the Prime Minister that any great calamity would befall the country if the Grand Trunk railway went into the hands of a receiver.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There might be a receiver appointed of the Grand Trunk proper. Then, suppose next week somebody applied for a receiver of one of the American lines that is an essential portion of the Grand Trunk system and of vital importance to this country; where would the receiver get the money required?
From the public as receiver.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: From the public? How would the receiver get money from the public?
He means the travelling public, I suppose.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
He would get all he could from the travelling public, but I am
afraid

The receiver would sell receivership certificates to the banks, or to the Dominion of Canada if you will, but those certificates would become a first charge on the Grand Trunk system. He

could still sell those securities, for surely they would be as good as or better than our securities against the road, being a first mortgage against the property. The world is not entirely dry of money.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not think the'hon. member would buy those certificates after a short time. In the first place, we have had to supply money for the receiver of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and we would have had to do the same in the case of the Grand Trunk.

We have not had to.
Where does the Dominion of Canada get its money?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Those receivership certificates would be a first charge perhaps on the Grand Trunk proper, but not on the subsidiary companies. Then what happens when a subsidiary company goes into receivership?-who is going to protect and save it?
The same thing happens.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The receiver would have to sell the road.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Never?
M. CAHILL: They rarely ever do.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There is no use pursuing that further.
There is every reason to pursue that question further. Dozens of roads in the United States have gone into the hands of receivers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And been sold.
All right. Let them be sold. What is wrong with that? The buyers are not going to pick the road up and take it away.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Very well; but if the road is sold and goes into the possession of another railway, is the hon. gentleman ready to face that contingency? And if he feels that the consequences are light and we can face them with equanimity, I suggest that he read a speech delivered in this House early in the spring of 1914 by the late right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier in relation to the consequences that would ensue from the Canadian Northern going into receivership. No one would suggest that the consequences would not be much worse in the case of the Grand Trunk. This system is far more compact and bigger, and the American part of it is far greater

proportionately. In every possible regard a'receivership would be far worse in its consequences. If he will read that speech he will easily come to the conclusion that that statesman at all events felt that it was well worth while to take every means in our power to prevent the consequences of a receivership even of the Canadian Northern.
I wish to read the letter, which is dated April 6-I was right as to the date-and is written by Mr. Kelley and Mr. Phippen to me:
Sir Alfred Smithers has requested us to reply to your cable to him of the 3rd instant. As you are aware, the subject matter of this cable has already been discussed at some length between the Hon. C. J. Doherty, Hon. J. D. Reid, Hon. J. A. Calder and Mr. E. i.. Newcombe, K.C., Deputy Minister of Justice, representing the Government, and the undersigned representatives of the company.
As discussed at that meeting, the arbitration agreement, which was entered into between the Government and the company and approved by a majority of the shareholders and afterwards ratified by an Act of the Parliament of Canada, provides that an award shall be made to determine the value of certain stocks which the Government undertakes to acquire, and that pending the making of this award, .certain powers usually exercised by the directors of the company shall be vested in a special committee to be appointed by the Government and the company, and that the remaining powers shall continue to be exercised by the directors until the final award is made. The agreement further provides that when this award has been made and the consideration paid, possession of the road shall be handed over by the company to the Government through the resignation of the directors and the appointment of a new Board. The agreement and legislation further provide that the holders of the outstanding debenture and guaranteed stocks of the company shall surrender their right to vote, and that the Government shall guarantee in perpetuity the payment of interest on these stocks. This guarantee, it may be noted, is not conditional on the com-' pletion of the arbitration, and would remain binding on Canada even if no award were ever made.
The agreement contemplates that the award will be made within nine months from the appointment of the arbitrators ; but as the length of time required for the completion of so complicated and important an investigation was necessarily a matter of conjecture, power was given under the legislation to the Council to provide any additional necessary time by an extension.
It is unnecessary to discuss the question of delay, which you appear to have raised in the House. Suffice it to say that the company absolutely denies any delay whatever on its part, either in the preparation or presentation of its case. The necessary preparation involved a detailed examination, listing and valuation of all of the physical assets of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada and of each of its subsidiaries, and of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and of each of its subsidiaries. as well as a critical investigation of the accounts of all of these companies, past as

well as present. Immediately it was known that an arbitration would be held, the accounting was placed in the hands of Messrs. Price, Waterhouse and Company, and the examination and valuation in the hands of Mr. J. B. Berry, a most experienced and competent engineer in suf h matters. Messrs. Price, Waterhouse and Company and Mr. Berry, and their respective staffs, although working continually, and often rive nights a weeks, were not able to complete the information required until the taking of evidence on the arbitration had well started. Since the day set for the commencement of the hearing-February 1,-the company has presented its evidence continuously, with the exception of two slight interruptins; one for half a day and the other for two days, to allow the auditors to complete the last of their reports.
It was pointed out at the meeting above referred to that it was the obvious duty of the Government to permit the agreed award to be made, and for this purpose to grant any extension of time which may be necessary, without seeking co alter the terms of the contract.
It was further pointed out that, under the terms, of the contract, the directors had no authority to .hand over possession of the property entrusted to them by the shareholders and confirmed by agreement with Parliament, without at least consulting the shareholders. Indeed, counsel were compelled to point out to the directors that should they attempt to hand over tli* property without adequate authority, they might be personally liable.	,
At the meeting referred to the undersigned expressed to the representatives of the Government the earnest desire of the directors to meet the wishes of the Government in every possible way, so far as that could be done legally and without sacrificing the interest of the shareholders'. They offered at once to have a meeting of the shareholders called and to submit any changes or modifications which the Government might desire made in the contract to the shareholders for their consideration and approval, and expressed the willingness of the directors to carry through any amendment which the shareholders might agree to.
The Government cannot, by its own failure to extend the time and obtain an award relieve :tself from its accepted responsibilities. Under these circumstances, we submit there is no alternative but that the Government grant the necessary extension to permit the making of the award, and in the meantime, as the agreement with the Government limits the powers of the company to finance its requirements, that the Government should continue as in the past to protect the company from being injured by such limitation.
The attitude of the board can probably best he shown by the following extract from a cable from Sir Alfred Smithers just received by Counsel :
"I repeat we are most anxious to help Govern

ment, and I again beg them to pay April 1 liabilities and thus give us time to do our ut-anost to meet Government consistently with our .legal rights and the shareholders' interest."

Has that obligation
ibeen met?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Not the April 1 obligation; the country was not liable on that. There was a payment on the 14th-I think it was-of April, upon which the company was liable. That was paid. There was
one in New York on a guarantee; that also was taken care of. Wherever we were liable, payment was made, but pending the transfer we have declined to do any Grand Trunk financing.
We have heen advised by cable from Sir A.lfred Smithers that with his approval it is your intention to lay all the correspondence relating to the Grand Trunk matter before the House this afternoon. We are sending you this letter by hand so that the file may be complete when tabled.
Howard Kelley,
F. P'. Phippen.
I replied to that as follows:
The letter sent by yourself and Mr. Phippen, dated April G, was duly acknowledged in mine of April 9. I have now only to add that the position of the Government in relation to the matters referred to in this letter is sufficiently set out in the antecedent correspondence.

I referred a moment ago to the American section of the Grand Trunk railway, at both ends, and my right hon. friend said that the Grand Trunk was a Canadian company and that there would be no difficulty in taking over the stock. Am I to understand that the American sections of the road are controlled by a Canadian company, not by American companies? I should like also to put another question to my right hon. friend. I have followed in the press the reports of the proceedings of the Arbitration Board. I noticed that there were some legal battles, but I could not help feeling that in a case involving millions and a property of immense extent, nine months was not such a long period of time within which to come to a decision. The reason why I mention it is that this morning I read in the Montreal Gazette about an arbitration case affecting the district of Montreal having reference to the famous Cedar Rapids on the St. Lawrence. 'I noticed that the award was made yesterday by Mr. Justice Tellier and by Professor Leleau, involving an amount of $125,000. Now, this is a case involving a large sum of money and an important question affecting riparian rights. The case opened several years ago and the arbitration has been in progress much longer than nine months. If the determination of a case of that nature, involving far less than the Grand Trunk question, occupied much longer than nine months, it seems to me that the Government might have extended at least a little longer the period within which the Grand Trunk Arbitration should be concluded. I know the right hon. gentleman will say that the Government are ready to extend the time, but subject to

their conditions. But does he not think that a limit of nine months is not such a long time for the consideration of a matter so important?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is a very important matter, one involving tremendous assets and tremendous sums of money, and, I understand, hundreds of thousands of people-
And a great responsibility.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
-and a great responsibility; there is no question about that. Ordinarily the Government should not be too exacting in the matter of just how many weeks should be taken to decide it. But the conditions were extraordinary. However, before I go on to that, I want to say that even though the number of shareholders, the amount involved, and the properties involved were immense, I do not think-giving my own personal opinion-that there was anything to prevent the arbitration being completed in the nine months. I say that deliberately after having the advantage of hearing argument between counsel on both sides and officials on both sides. One extra-. ordinary feature of it is this: The Government first of all, having had some experience in the matter, felt that six months would be sufficient. At the request of the Grand Trunk-I think they asked for something more at first; anyway, it was extended to nine; and that extension was made not merely as a start but in the belief on the part of both parties that that time would be sufficient. Now, the Government got its experts-chiefly engineers and expert railway men-and its legal staff, to meet the Grand Trunk's case. We knew that, naturally, there would be no resource and no skill purchasable that the Grand Trunk would not acquire, if they could, to make their case. We procured a legal and expert engineering staff sufficient to get the material and the evidence and finish the work in the time stipulated. If we had felt that more time would be necessary or would be asked for, we would have had a smaller staff and would have incurred less expense. After doing that, it was the conviction of counsel for the Government, and after hearing argument it was my conviction, that no serious attempt was made to complete the arbitration within the stipulated time. I am pretty sure that if the hon. member would read certain reports made to the Government by counsel connected with the case, he would come to that conclusion. I have here a report from Mr. Tilley to Mr. New-
combe dated March 31, and an earlier one dated March 19.

Could my right hon.
friend, without reading the letters, give the purport of them?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, I think I could
give that, subject to correction as to dates. The arbitrators were appointed on June 9. Previous to that it was known that the agreement was to be made, and the Grand Trunk naturally set to work-we know this-to	get their evidence ready.
This was a considerable time before we could do so-about a year before. They were in the offices; they had access to everything. We had to get what we wanted, merely by requisition, by going in and asking for it. Notwithstanding that, when the arbitrators met on September 1, our side was all ready to go on; but the Grand Trunk representatives came totally unprepared, and asked for an adjournment until November. They also requested a physical examination of the system and that request was yielded to by the arbitrators; but when November came, they were no more ready then, although our counsel had been ready in September, and they asked for an adjournment to February 1. It seems very hard to credit the fact that Government counsel, having started preparation many months later than the Grand Trunk, should be amply prepared by September, while the Grand Trunk counsel, who started many months earlier, could not be prepared by September, and had to have an adjournment to November and another adjournment to February. When February 1 came-I do not know that I would be justified in saying how their case was conducted; that would be a matter more for the arbitrators to say- but looking on from outside, and reading the reports that I got and from certain of the evidence that I saw, I was not impressed that the Grand Trunk was animated by any exceeding enthusiasm to expedite the arbitration. I do not know whether the description by Mr. Tilley of the way in which it was conducted was justified or not; I have no word of comment to make on that; but anyway it proceeded until April 9 was reached. And even then the Grand Trunk had not its case in, and not a day was left for the Government to put in its case. Under those circumstances, I think the fair conclusion is that no serious attempt was made to comply with the provisions of section 8 of the agreement in that regard, or, at least, no sufficient attempt.

What are the extraordinary circumstances that justify a refusal to grant an extension? We had agreed at once to a certain portion of the consideration, that is to say, to guaranteeing the underlying securities, and it was the remaining portion that was subject to arbitration. Whatever the arbitrators found, we were bound to pay. Under the ordinary law, the property should have been ours at first. We felt that even though the directors might possibly convince the arbitration board and others that they had proceeded sufficiently rapidly, they could not convince anybody that they needed to stay any longer in possession for the sake of procuring their evidence, and that they should then have consented to give us the property. They were informed in abundant time to have obtained consent from their shareholders; but instead of doing that and meeting the Government in as fair a way as we thought we had met them, they distinctly and promptly refused, gave no consideration to the matter at all. As April 9 approached, instead of an attitude of co-operation, there was more evidence of propaganda in England to create resentment in the minds of shareholders and others against the conduct of the Government. Under those circumstances we did not feel that we should step down from our position, merely because they then came along and told us that the shareholders had not been called; that April 9 had arrived and they had not the power and they argued from that that we were very unreasonable in asking them to give us possession when they had not power to do so. The circumstances are unusual for the chief reason that they were calling upon us to provide the money to finance the road and claiming that we had to do it because of the agreement. The agreement does not say that we had to provide the money to finance the road. The agreement says that we may provide the money if that is essential. The primary obligation is on them. They might have come with a pretty strong position if they had said: "We are running the road; we are taking care of it; there is no reason why you should not extend the arbitration." But they were not in that position.
What about the first part of the question as regards the American companies?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The American roads are run by the directors of those roads, but the directors of those roads are nominees of the Grand Trunk. Some of the roads are held on long-term leases.

The directors are
nominees of the present company?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, and, in effect, the ultimate owners are the Grand Trunk.

The first clause at line 31 reads:
The directors.... shall resign or vacate their offices as directors at such time or times and in such manner as may be requested by the Government.
There is nothing to show how that request is to be made or what notice is to be given, and it struck me that that might operate as a cause of delay unless something was inserted to show that, such as the filing of a request at the head office of the company in Canada, or some such wording as that.
In subclause (b) on page 2, there is clearly a clerical error. Subclause (a) reads:
Nominees of the Government shall be duly appointed to the vacancies caused thereby.
And so forth: Subclause (b) reads:
The directors of the company so nominated by the Government and their successors.
That is clearly a clerical error. It should read:	"so appointed." It would be absurd
to speak of men who are only nominated, and their successors. The word "appointed" seems to be required in place of the word "nominated."
I notice the phraseology in regard to the appointment of directors is not the same in subclause (c) as in subclauses (b) and (d). Subclause (c) reads:
That the meetings of the hoard of directors of the company for the transaction of any business may be validly held in Canada or elsewhere.
The other subclauses refer to the "said board" or the "board to be appointed." Therefore, I think the wording would be clearer and the agreement more intelligible if subclause (c) read:
That the meetings of the new board of directors of the company-
Or,
That the meetings of the board of directors of the company so appointed-
And so on.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I will have the points looked into. As to the first, the Governor in Council would have to notify the Grand Trunk at its head office. The Governor in Council would act by Order in Council, and that would be sent at once to the Grand Trunk. That would be the usual way in which the matter would be carried

out. The second point seems to me to be well worth considering', and the third as well. I will have that done before we get through.

As regards the point just
raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Morphy), I notice the wording "shall be duly appointed." I presume that means shall be appointed by the Government because by subclause (b) of the agreement the shareholders do not exercise any powers of voting or choosing after this agreement has come into force. The shareholders have abrogated all their powers of action by the agreement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
"Duly" means simply
"in the proper way." If they are nominees of the Government, they could not be nominees of the shareholders. I do not see that "duly" is necessary. I think the only effect of it there is "to be appointed the way nominees of the Government should be appointed." I shall have that point noted too.
I have not read the Bill very closely, but if there is a mode of appointment provided in the Bill, they should be appointed in that way.

The powers which the Government are asking under this Bill are certainly rather unusual. The Government is, in effect, saying that before these arbitration proceedings may be resumed the owners of the railway must hand over the control and operation of the road in its entirety to the Government. I think my right hon. friend the Prime Minister has presented a pretty strong case to the House why that unusual proceeding should be taken. Undoubtedly, we must assume that the Government have been in close touch with the situation. They are familiar with all the circumstances; they have been living with it from day to day in a manner that the ordinary member of this House has not had an opportunity to do, and I for one feel like taking the position that if they say this is necessary in the public interest, the responsibility is theirs, and I am not disposed to put anything in the way of their getting the powers they ask. The whole question is full of difficulties. I am bound to say that I can come to no other conclusion than that there has been a lack of frank co-operation, to say the least, on the part of the Grand Trunk Railway. I think that is a fair position to take. There is no doubt that if we go back over the history leading up to this whole difficulty
[Hr. Meighen.]
the Grand Trunk have, in a very large measure, indeed, their share of blame for the present situation. At the inception of the National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Government of the day undertook the consideration of that project, if my information is correct, and my authority is the Drayton-Acworth report, at the instance of the Grand Trunk Railway. Certainly, very generous assistance was given to that enterprise by the Government. It built the National Transcontinental, at a cost to this country of $160,000,000 or $170,000,000. It gave liberal guarantees on the Grand Trunk Pacific, which was the creation of the old Grand Trunk railway. As soon as the National Transcontinental was completed, the Grand Trunk, for reasons which we do not need to discuss here, declined to accept its responsibility of operating that road. It has, since the completion of the Grand Trunk Pacific, sought by every possible means to avoid its obligations in respect of that portion of the system. I am quite within the bounds of fact in making that statement.
It may be said that the proper course to have pursued in this matter was to have let the Grand Trunk Railway go into liquidation. I think there are serious difficulties in the way of that proceeding having regard to the public interest of this country, and I find myself a good deal in agreement with the statement made by the Prime Minister in that respect. If this Grank Trunk system was one company alone, then possibly that way might have been considered, but as a matter of fact, it is not one company; it is composed of many independent companies, linked up together by a system of finance that has gone on for two generations in its administration. Under those circumstances, if each of these individual companies was allowed to go into liquidation, when the whole proceedings were terminated and the liquidation was complete, the result would be that the entire system that has been built up in years would be disintegrated. The National Transcontinental and tire Grand Trunk Pacific enterprise was undertaken for the specific purpose of rounding out the old Grand Trunk Railway system in Eastern Canada. The one was complementary to the other, and I have always felt in respect of this matter that since we have the National Transcontinental on our hands, since by virtue of the guarantees this country gave on the Grand Trunk Pacific that road is also back on

our hands, there was only one course to pursue, if it could be pursued, and that was that the whole Grand Trunk system should be taken over to carry out the original intention of having a national system in its entirety. Under those circumstances, while the way has been difficult, while there have been a great many dark clouds overhanging the whole proceedings as far as its financial aspect is concerned, nevertheless, it does appeal to me that no other course is open to us in the best interests) of this country than by ,every reasonable means to secure control of the Grand Trunk Railway and incorporate it in the national system.
