Otherwise, we would simply have a transcontinental line, beginning at one end of the country and ending at the other, with nothing to feed it in Eastern Canada and no matter what disposition we may wish to make ultimately of our National Railway system this is vital. I have my own views on that subject, but I shall not give them to the House now except to say that there is no other course open to us to follow but to continue operating these roads as a National Railway system. To those who think we should dispose of the roads and turn them over to a private company, I put the question: What position would we be in if we at>-tempted to sell to a private company a transcontinental railway that began at the Pacific and ended near the Atlantic without any feeders to support it? We would be at a hopeless disadvantage in trying to dispose of it as a business proposition. So ho matter what final disposition we make of these roads, it is essential, indeed vital, that the whole be linked up together in one comprehensive system. While, as I said at the opening of my re-
5 p.m. marks, the Government are ask-in this legislation for powers that are to my mind quite extraordinary, nevertheless, from the .information they have given us, and from their intimate knowledge of the situation which possibly other hon. members cannot have, I feel disposed to put nothing in their way in the passage of this legislation, and, of course, the responsibility is the Government's for bringing this matter before the House.

I appreciate the very great difficulty of the Government in handling this railway problem, and I confess at the moment I have a great deal of difficulty myself in reaching a conclusion as to what is the best course to pursue. I

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
am rather more anxious to seek light than 'to offer suggestions or to criticise, and anything I say now is by way of offering a point for the consideration of the Government, and not as expressing any adverse criticism.
I am going to ask attention for a moment to the consideration of how this transaction will look in England. Some will tell us that they do not care how it looks in England. I grant at once that it is more important for us to be right, and to feel that we are right, than to consider how they do these things in England. Still, that is a view that ought to be expressed with some qualification, for this reason. In a general way we are anxious to stand well with all countries in the world, and particularly anxious to stand well with England, even in financial matters. I would not have it understood for a moment that I concur in the criticisms that are being offered in England to-day as to the attitude of this Government. I know that English shareholders, perhaps all kinds of shareholders, when they come to deal with the Government are easily persuaded that their condition is one of martyrdom, and that they are being harshly_ treated.^ I know the proneness of the English financial press to get behind the English shareholder and to put the notion in his head that he has a grievance. Therefore, I discount to a considerable extent what is being said today in the English press. I agree with the Prime Minister in this, that we ought to be sure that we stand on safe ground in this matter, that whatever the consequences may be, we will know that an effort has been made to make the best of the situation.
Now what is the point of difference between the Government and the Grand Trunk Company? In reality, it is a very small one. Again, I say, I am not agreeing with the Grand Trunk's position; I am inviting the attention of my right hon. friend to this particular thought, what is the point of difference to-day between the Grand Trunk and the Government? It is a matter of three months' extension. Is not that all?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That might at first
sight appear to be all, but in view of the evident intention to appeal, it might be more a matter of years than of months.
The agreement of last year allows nine months for the arbitration, and I think there is force in the suggestion of the hon. member for Maison-

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
neuve (Mr. Lemieux), that that is not a long time, after all. I recollect, in the course of the long discussion of this matter, suggesting myself that a transaction of this nature would necessarily occupy a considerable length of time, and I did not think that nine months would be too long. I am not going to enter into the question whether or not the Grand Trunk, generally speaking, have been dilatory or otherwise, but I again point out the inadequacy of nine months. It must have been contemplated that there was a possibility that nine months would not be sufficient, because the Government included a clause taking power to themselves to extend the time. It is evident that they considered nine months would not be be long enough. And when the time came and the Grand Trunk asked for an extension the Government refused. There was a time when the Government, under my right hon. friend the late Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), probably treated the Grand Trunk harshly, hut I do not want to go into that. It raises old questions which are not relevant to his debate. But I do not say that the Grand Trunk were treated harshly in the last agreement, which, I think, was more generous to them than to the people of Canada. Nevertheless, the agreement was finally decided upon by the action of this Parliament. The only point of difference that has arisen since the passage of the legislation of last year is the request of the Grand Trunk company for three months' extension of time; there is no getting away from that. And the case will present itself to the shareholders in England in this way: The Grand Trunk Company were allowed nine months, and as that time did not prove adequate, they asked for three months' extension and the Government flatly refused it. Now, that is a pretty strong case t6 present to the English shareholders; it is a forceful case to submit to the editors of English financial papers, and I am a little afraid that when that case is presented in that form there will be a good deal of strong public feeling in England, for the shareholders will feel that the company have been treated pretty harshly. It is a purely technical question whether they should have nine months or twelve months, and it will be felt that the Government has acted rather severely in holding the company rigidly to the nine months. I think that if I were a financial journalist in London I could make a strong case against Canada on that point; and we are concerned that no strong case shall be made against us, notwithstanding what 
some people suggest, that we do not care what the English press or the English financiers say. We ought to care what they say. At present we are not borrowing money in England, but the time is not far distant when we shall be mighty glad 'o do so, and when we shall find it necessary to go to England for the purpose. So that it behooves us to maintain our reputation and our credit. I am not offering these observations in any critical spirit, but I think I have stated the case as it will be presented to the English shareholders. It will be confined to that one consideration. The English shareholders will not go into all the old questions and discussions regarding the Grand Trunk Pacific or any other matter of that kind. They will say:' All these matters were settled by the Act of 1920, and we were allowed nine months; but as the obligation was a tremendous one, and, as the Government obviously anticipated, nine months was not a sufficient time, and the company asked for an extension of three months, which was refused, the Government taking the position that they would grant this extension on condition that the whole property should be surrendered. I am afraid that this is not a strong position for the Government to take in the eye of the English shareholders. I repeat, I do not say this in any spirit of antagonism, because I fully realize the difficult situation in which the Government find themselves; but I do ask them seriously to ponder this particular thought.

I should not like to prejudice the English shareholder or any other shareholder in connection with any property in which they may have invested money in Canada, because I should dislike to have my own investments prejudiced by the Government. I disagree, however, with the suggestion that we are refusing to carry out the arbitration. We simply say that if an extension of time for the arbitration is to be granted we must have possession of the road. Why? Because the road is being managed now partially by Government representatives and partially by representatives of the Grand Trunk, and it strikes me that the situation is a good deal like the manager of a business who knows that at the end of three months or six months his management will cease. He naturally does not look after the interests of the business as he would if he knew that at the end of six months his salary would be increased instead of his services being dispensed with. So that it is absolutely vital that the Government

24G1
should take over the road. I entirely agree with my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar), that it is useless having these other roads as national roads, without the old Grand Trunk as a feeder, because the original intention was that these roads were to be operated by the old Grand Trunk. The intention as regards the building of these other roads might have been all right, but in my judgment the time was inopportune. That, however, does not affect the present situation, and I say that to complete the national roads we must have the old Grand Trunk lines as feeders; otherwise we shall have a national road with one end in the air, so to speak. Now, we are not demanding that the Grand Trunk shall sacrifice anything in the world. Surely in nine months they should have all the papers and documents, all the facts and everything that is possible or that can imaginably be necessary, to complete their arbitration. Because, in the first place, they themselves are in possession of the facts. As the Prime Minister has pointed out, the Government are the ones who are at a disadvantage in the collection of facts in connection with the arbitration, and that statement seems very reasonable to me. The Grand Trunk themselves had all the facts in their possession, and there was nothing in connection with the whole case that they could easily get hold off. Surely, therefore, they do not want more time than nine months. We do not ask them to sacrifice anything in the arbitration; we only ask them to hand over the road to Government management in the meantime, and we shall continue the arbitration. As to letting the roads go into liquidation and appointing receivers, we should have applications for receivers from every one of the subsidiaries of the Grand Trunk-
No.

That would be the case, and what a fine mess we would be in before we got through. There would be no benefit to the lines we already own, and I repeat that we must have the Grand Trunk as it is now, to complete the Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific. The old Grand Trunk touches nearly every hamlet in Ontario, and it would be a very valuable acquisition to any one who could properly manage a railway. I have always been an opponent of Government ownership of railways and of everything else, but I did support the taking over of the old Grand Trunk, because it would complete our system of national railways. The Govern-
156i
ment, I think, have been perfectly reasonable and generous in their treatment of the shareholders of the Grand Trunk, and it is nothing but absolute good reason and common sense to ask them, if the arbitration is to be continued, to hand over the road to Government management in the meantime.

I would ask the Prime
Minister a question, which possibly he has already answered. So far as I am personally concerned, the information would assist me, to some extent at least, in arriving at a decision. That question is, whether the fact that the period of arbitration has exceeded nine months does in effect vitiate or render voidable the agreement that was made when it was first decided to acquire the Grand Trunk? If there is any likelihood that the agreement is rendered void or voidable, then we might have to decide whether we shall continue with the arbitration under the conditions of this Bill, or whether the road shall be allowed to go into liquidation and into the hands of a receiver, as has been suggested by one or two members-a procedure of which I, personally, do not approve, for the reasons that have been given by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) and the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt). I agree with them that in order to make the national system a success it is absolutely necessary that we shall have the Grand Trunk Railway system as well, but the matter might be debatable on the ground as to what action should be taken now- whether the road shall be allowed to go to the wall, if you like, and the Government later acquire it if it can, at whatever price it may be able to get it at, or whether we shall go on with the arbitration as provided for in the Bill.
The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) has raised another point, that it might be well to extend the period of arbitration for three months. Personally, I am not in sympathy with that suggestion. It seems to me that the investors in England, the holders of the bonds, the holders of the underlying securities, are already absolutely protected because the Government has already agreed to take over those liabilities. As to the arbitration of the common stock it does not seem to me that prejudices any one very seriously. My own opinion at the time it was agreed to arbitrate was that the Government made an error in this way-that we should have arbitrated all the securities

of the Grand Trunk, and not merely the stocks which are now under arbitration, and it was for that reason, and for that reason only, that I voted against the Bill at that time. I was in favour of the acquisition of the Grand Trunk, hut I did feel that under the conditions, seeing that the whole proposition was not to be arbitrated, the people of Canada were likely to be called upon to pay too much for the railway, and I am still of that opinion. As to the shareholders-outside of the ordinary holders of the underlying securities-I cannot see that they have any very good ground for objecting, in view of the fact that the Government is actually under the necessity of supplying funds. It seems to me it is only fair that the Government of Canada, who are going to supply large sums of money for the carrying on of the railway, might very well demand that the system come under their control. That is my position. I would like to know from the minister whether, in his opinion or in the opinion of the Department of Justice, the agreement itself could possibly be voided by reason of the delay in the completion of the arbitration beyond the nine months originally fixed. If there is no possible escape from it, then I can see no reason why we should not go on with the Bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I gave an answer to
the question, but I do not think the hon. member was present at the time. There are many legal questions that may be put

many that I would not like to take the responsibility of answering in any way. But even were I to assume that responsibility, there are very many as to which one cannot answer "yes" or "no." The hon. member asks: Does the agreement stand or has it fallen-has either party to it any obligations now? Well, in respect to the arbitration, which was the main purpose of the agreement, it has fallen. I give that as my opinion. There can be no further arbitration, without the intervention of Parliament, and there can be no further arbitration resting on the foundation of the agreement alone.

May I ask the Prime
Minister this further question: should the Government decline to continue with this Bill what would be the outcome?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There can be no further arbitration.

The whole agreement
would be void.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Now, I am coming to
that. The arbitration was the main purpose of the agreement. In such a contingency as the hon. member suggests the agreement is at an end, there can be no more arbitration. Now is there any section of the agreement, or any portion of it, that still is valid-that is to say is there any obligation on either, party, aside altogether from the arbitration, based.upon the agreement? Well, the Grand Trunk claims there is, as seen by the letter which I read. It claims that the Government guarantee of the debenture and guaranteed stock-practically all the mortgage securities-is valid, anyway, whether the arbitration falls or whether it does not.
Will my right hon. friend pardon me? Do the Government not practically admit that, by their action in having paid certain obligations since, the period of arbitration has expired?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, the Government
does not admit it, but takes this position. It has always been ready, and is ready today, to take the road at the price of those securities-always ready-consequently, the question does not arise; at any rate we do not admit it has arisen in such form that we need dispute it, and we feel that it is better for the credit of Canada that we should pay those obligations because, at least, it might be argued that we are liable anyway. Nor do we shun the liability; we are quite prepared to take the road at that price. To shun it would mean the sacrifice of some hundreds of millions of money- perhaps I should not say "hundreds of millions," but a hundred of millions of money -that has been invested in the road and has rendered service to the people of Canada. We have not suggested getting the road at any lesser price than that. The hon. member says we should originally have put in arbitration these underlying securities as well as the preference and common stocks of the company. But under the circumstances, the Government felt it was its duty to acquire the whole property. Suppose that property, instead of being a railway system, had been a farm and there was a mortgage against that farm of, say, $10,000, and we said to the owners, "We will take that property and assume the mortgage and we will arbitrate with you on the equity of redemption. We will arbitrate with you as to what we will pay over and above that mortgage." We have done just the same here.
But you would not take a farm that was not worth as much as the mortgage?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We do not suggest
taking the property at less than the value of these underlying securities; we did not think there was any need of doing so at all -we would not have been any further ahead. What we promptly said is this: "We will assume these underlying securities but we will arbitrate as to the value of the equity of redemption represented by the three preference stocks and the common stocks"-on which there had been placed a value of some hundreds of millions of dollars. Surely that was a pretty reasonable position?	[DOT]
The mere fact that such a sum of money had been placed in them does not imply that the value is still there.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I know that it does not imply it, but we all know the Grand Trunk railway, and we all know the advantages to this country to have that system which is so vital to our own commercial existence, and we did not think it would add very much to the reputation of this country if we said to the owners of these securities-men who started together seventy or eighty years ago and had put their money into this railway system in Canada-if we said to them "No, we won't even assume the underlying securities, we won't even admit your property is worth that, but we will put them in jeopardy under arbitration as well." We did not think it would be wise to do that, and in order to bring about an amicable arrangement along the desired lines we said, "We will assume these securities and arbitrate about the rest." We are taking that position consistently still.

Do we understand
then that if this arbitration falls down completely the whole deal is off, or if it is not off that the Government will get the property at the price of the underlying securities?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If the arbitration falls down, then, as I see the circumstances before me, if nothing else takes place the whole property marches right into liquidation with all the consequences attendant upon that. I do not say that nothing should be done to protect the property and hold it intact and not let it go into liquidation, but I do say that before this Parliament undertakes to do that we should seek to
carry out the intent of the original agreement, we should exercise every means in our power to put it out of the power of the holders of these securities to say we treated them unfairly. But I believe that something could be done which is well within the authority of Parliament to do, to see still that the dissipation and all the consequences of liquidation, as it would take place under the present law, did not ensue.
Would the right hon. gentleman-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I should have answered the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, but the other questions intervened. The hon. member apprehends that there may be some cause of complaint on the part of owners of Grand Trunk stocks, in that although they had made an agreement providing for a nine months' arbitration, and in that the agreement contemplated the possibility of an extension, yet they have been denied an extension of three months, that being all that was applied for. Now,
I do not think they have any cause of complaint at all. I fully agree with the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's that it is of the utmost importance to this country to be sure that we are quite scrupulous in our dealings with the Grand Trunk shareholders. I also thoroughly understand this, that we are very likely to see the matter from our point of view instead of theirs. I realized that very fully when I came in contact" with Grand Trunk directors in England, in 1918. They look on this whole situation from an entirely different standpoint-they are away off somewhere on what does not seem to me tenable ground at all. But knowing we are at a different standpoint from theirs, it is doubly important that we be even more than usually scrupulous in regard to our treatment of those shareholders.	[DOT]
Now, the way the Government argued the matter is this. It is true the Grand Trunk company only intimated a need for a three months' extension. It is also true that the whole arbitration might have been over in the three months. But several other factors of the problem came up. First of all, and very important, the Grand Trunk directorate found themselves unable to carry out their primary responsibility to finance the system, and they were under the necessity of continually calling upon the Government to furnish moneys to hold their system together. Secondly, they said to us: " Yes, we are only asking for three

months, but we intend to appeal this case. We tell you right away that we are going to take it to the Supreme Court, and if that does not satisfy us we are going to take it to the Privy Council." What does all that mean? It means three months with them in possession of the road, and in a position to fix salaries and everything else as directors of the system can do; and when the three months are up, suppose the arbitration is not over? Then they will want another extension. But suppose it is over, and the award is made? They have their appeal entered, and before it is finally determined it might be two years longer. In the meantime they are in possession of the system of railways for which the country has paid in large measure, and which is equitably ours, and they are in a position to dictate everything-and it is a great deal-connected with the operation of a great railyaw system. We thought the time to speak was now. The system should be in our hands to-day. If the three months expired and the award were given, it would not be in our hands, for we then would have to wait for the determination of the appeal that followed the award.

Might I pursue that thought for a moment more? I have carefully refrained from expressing any opposition to the meaure or any adverse criticism. I have tried to put myself for reasons that I have stated, in the position of the British shareholder-not in respect to the unreasonable complaint which very often English shareholders will make regarding colonial investments or investments in overseas countries, but in the position of the reasonable shareholder; I am trying to see how he will look at this thing and how he will present it to his fellow shareholders and to the English financial public. Now, my right hon. friend says that the Grand Trunk are going to appeal. Well, that is not a ground for complaint. The agreement gives them the right to appeal.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Correct.

May I ask my hon.
friend if the Grand Trunk are asking the Government of Canada to advance millions of dollars, something that was not contemplated when the agreement was entered into?

I think it would have been better if the Government had based their action on the fact that they would refuse to finance the company. I think the demand for immediate possession without extension of time for the arbitration is rather a weakness; but if they had said:

"We will give you an extension of time, but we will not give you any more money,"
I think they would have taken a very much stronger position than they did take.

It must be remembered in dealing with this case that we are dealing on behalf of Canada with very adroit and powerful negotiators, and unless the course the Government intimate they are going to take is wrong, it seems to me that, generally speaking, we should back them up. So far I feel, and I think the people of Canada feel, that Canada's case has been ably conducted by the ministers in charge, and I think that very fact should make us go slow in limiting them in the course which they now tell us they think is proper.
It must be remembered that this agreement with the Grand Trunk following the legislation was one of compromise-it must necessarily have been so. This very clause providing for arbitration and allowing the Grand Trunk to remain in possession of their property pending the arbitration was, as we were told last year, put in only on the very strong pleading of the Grand Trunk itself, because its directors said: "We cannot conduct this arbitration to our advantage or with the success we are entitled to if we have the property taken out of our hands." As a matter of fact, the Government could have taken the property at that time and let the arbitration go on without it, but in giving away here and taking as much as you can there -the usual course of negotiations between astute negotiators-the Government gave way on this particular point.
Now, I do not agree that there is anything here of a harsh nature as is referred to by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's, I do not think there is even a suspicion of it, and I do not share his feeling that the shareholders in England have any cause for criticism or dissatisfaction. Nine months is a long time to prepare for an arbitration. It has been said here, and there is no contradiction of it, that for a year, or perhaps more than that, the Grand Trunk was getting ready for this very thing. In addition to that, we have the fact that some months ago the Government intimated to the Grand Trunk that time was passing and that the arbitration would have to fee terminated on the 9th of April. But up to the time this notice was given-I think it was in January-practically nothing had been done; everything had been left at loose
ends. I do not know whether it was by design or through carelessness. I do think that the English investors and shareholders, who are by no means fools, will find out where the fault was, and when they come to the end of their investigation they will not criticize the Government of Canada. The company have themselves to blame if they are in default. As the Prime Minister said, they must have been dilatory or they could have been well on with their work and have had it concluded by this time. It was never necessary that they should have the property in their hands pending the arbitration. The stock, which represents the property, belongs to Canada; the system itself was left with the Grand Trunk as the result of a compromise which they demanded. I think, therefore, that there is nothing harsh in the Government's action. I am not disposed to be influenced by propaganda in England. The cleverest propaganda carried on in business is that which is carried on in England. They have their important newspapers, the editors of which are clever, successful business men, and the moment some difficulty is seen there is a flood of comments, well printed and well edited articles, appearing in these papers, to influence public opinion. If we are sure we are right, we should not bother ourselves about what is said by the English newspapers in regard to this matter. This afternoon I see a despatch quoting the view of no less a person than the financial editor of the Times, who is right at the pinnacle of newspaper ability in the Old Country. The despatch says:
The financial editor of the Times understands that the Grand Trunk Railway Board have decided to give favorable consideration to the proposals contained in the new bill before the Canadian Parliament for the acquisition of the. railway, provided certain conditions in connection with the arbitration proceedings are fulfilled. Presumably, says the Times, the transfer of the control of the railway to thfe Canadian Government, which has shown a considerable capacity to assimilate railways in difficulties, would mean that the Canadian Government would find the money to pay the interest arrears, and take steps to assure the resumption of the arbitration proceedings without delay.
There you have the whole thing; the moment they are met with firmness and ability, there is indignation, but as the financial editor of the Times says, there is evidently a feeling now of willingness to come to terms. But the English shareholders will be in no way prejudiced by this Bill, because the arbitration can resume at once. It came to an end, not at the

instance of the Government but at the instance of the arbitrators themselves. Sir Walter Cassels ruled that the arbitration was bound by the terms of the statute, and in that ruling his colleagues on the board concurred. So we should put this legislation through, enabling us to resume negotiations with the company, and we can do so without tlie slightest feeling that any injustice is being done.
The member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) asked why we should not let this system go into the hands of a receiver. Now, to the timid and over-cautions people of the country, to whom, I suppose, my hon. friend and some of his colleagues on the other side wish to appeal as part of the political end of these negotiations, that is a very good argument. These people say: Why should we assume ownership of this system? Let it go into the hands of a receiver. But what is a receiver? A receiver is a person appointed by a court to take over a property pending the satisfaction of the debt by the sale of the property. Sometimes shareholders themselves appoint one person or a committee of shareholders to take over the property, as they are entitled to do under their bonds, and that is sometimes called receivership. But we must take care not to use the word "receiver" loosely; it involves court action. Now, what is the position of a creditor in dealing with the Grand Trunk system? It must be remembered that the Grand Trunk system differs very widely from the Grand Trunk congeries of companies. The rights of the shareholders against any one of the - companies making up the Grand Trunk system exist under their bond. I have not before me the terms of the bond mortage which is the security for investment in the case of these different companies, but I should be very much surprised if it con-'tained any provision for a receiver. Why? Because only the court can appoint a receiver. The only way that the shareholders can satisfy themselves under the bond mortgage is by taking over the property, provided there is a clause to that effect. What happens, in this case? They appoint a committee of the shareholders to take over the property and manage it, but there is no such thing as a receiver. If instead of taking over the property they went to the proper tribunal and asked that the bond obligation should be merged into a judgment obligation, then they could ask the court to appoint a receiver temporarily, to hold the property until the judgment was satisfied by execution and sale. But it 
is not the system that falls into the hands of a receiver ; it is each particular company making up the system. You would have the court dealing with the companies, putting each company into the hands of a receiver for the time being and gradually proceeding to sell the property. Then we would have the companies dissolved and broken up, and we would have a rival company which desired one particular part of the system to be sold under the judgment of the court against one of the companies, making a bid, acquiring the line and destroying the system as a whole. Canada would suffer if such a course were pursued; the Government must guard against having the Grand Trunk system brought to an end piecemeal in that way. When my hon. friend speaks about putting in a receiver, as is sometimes done in the United States, he must bear in mind the difference between the laws of the United States and the laws of Canada and the difference between the wording of the different bonds. While it is true that receivers have been appointed in the United States for bankrupt railways, almost always it has been the result not of antagonism, but of agreement between the directors, the company itself and the shareholders. So it would be unfair to assume that we could put these companies in the hands of a receiver. Receivership is a temporary thing, to protect the property until judgment can be settled by sale. By no means could the Grand Trunk system be operated under a receiver for more than a very temporary period. It would be suicidal for us to submit to temporary management through receivership.
The hon. member speaks of the bonds. Can he tell me of any terminable bonds issued by the Grand Trunk?
I have not them before me. If I had been prepared for this, I would have looked the matter up and would give the hon. gentleman the best answer I could. I am speaking of the ordinary bonds.

There are no ordinary
bonds.

I presume they have all a fairly similar character. I am talking now of what is to be done in case of default by the Grand Trunk system, which default means the Grand Trunk defaulting by its different companies. It would be a dangerous thing to sell each of those different companies at one time, because you would

only have a temporary receivership which my hon. friend seems to covet or desire or believe in. The ultimate and inevitable result of proceeding's under a bond mortgage is the sale of the property, unless the bondholders take the property over themselves, and that is very seldom done, because the result of management by bondholders of commercial institutions has been disastrous on this continent, perhaps ever since such management has been attempted. No committee of bondholders has ever been able, so far as I can remember, successfully to run a railway. Therefore, we must bear in mind that the result of action by bondholders of the different companies will mean sale of the different companies separately. There would be offers for some of the companies which would be useful to other and rival railways, and the other companies composing the system would remain inactive for want of buyers to conduct them. We cannot go into this whole question without remembering that the Grand Trunk is a system and not a company and that, being a system, it must be protected as a system. Therefore, it seems to me that this proposed legislation, which is not unjust to the Grand Trunk, but which will have the effect of bringing them to the very point of negotiation which is indicated in the Times article printed in to-day's papers, is the wise course to take at the present time.

Having heard from the fount of wisdom, whence the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) drew the inspiration for the speech which he delivered at Toronto a few days ago, and which was adverted to this afternoon by some hon. members on this side-a speech, I understand, calculated to secure a Tory re-nomination for the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat)-may I be permitted to return to a practical feature of the issue that we are discussing? One of the points dealt with by the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) might be made more clear to the committee if he would have the goodness to address himself to it again for a moment. The period of the arbitration and the time for making the award expired on April 9. The right hon. gentleman has read to the committee this afternoon correspondence not included in the file originally brought down, showing that on April 6 the right hon. gentleman and his Government had in their hands what was practically the ultimatum of the Grand Trunk Railway Company with
reference to the arbitration. May I inquire why, immediately upon the receipt of that correspondence, action was not taken to extend the time for the arbitration?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Because the Government does not necessarily yield when an ultimatum is presented. The letter of April 6 offered no new material to change the position which the Government had taken. In fact, the Government does not by any means agree in every respect with the position taken in that letter.
What I desire to know is-was it on account of a desire to secure control that action was not taken prior to April 9?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It was because the Government had decided that a condition of extension must be possession of the system.

I understand that, under the agreement of 1909, it was provided that as soon as the management committee took charge of the road, the voting power in respect of the debenture stock- I think also the guaranteed stock-should cease. What was the voting power in respect of the debenture stock and the guaranteed stock, which amounted to many millions of dollars, and what is the proportion of votes of those stocks as compared with the whole voting power of the company?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The relative voting strength, which I
have just received, is as follows:

That means this that the preference and guarantee together amount to 1,024,720 votes and the debenture stock to 1,161,952 votes, so that the debenture stock votes are more than the total votes for the preference and guaranteed stock. Added to that there are the common stock votes, 479,108.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have done so, and
the total is 1,024,720 votes.

It should be included
with the debenture stock, not with the preference.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member is right. In this table it is with the preference stock. The guaranteed stock anyway is represented by 500,000 votes; the debenture stock by 1,161,952 votes; so that the two together would be represented by 1,661,952 votes, as against preference stock represented by 524,720 votes, ordinary stock represented by 479,108 votes, or a total of about 1,000,000 votes. The guaranteed and the debenture stock have the majority.

As a matter of fact we are, if not in law, in equity the owners and really entitled to representation on these two stocks, the debenture stock and the guaranteed stock. As a matter of equity, we control the majority of the voting power in the Grand Trunk Pacific, and had not the Act provided that when the committee took over the management the voting power ceased, the voting power would have gone to the Dominion Government, and the Dominion Government would have controlled the majority of the voting power. I do not know if we control that now, because the

agreement provides that there shall not be voting power in respect of this stock, when guaranted by the Government but as a matter of equity we are more interested in the management of the affairs of the company than the other shareholders, and if we had the voting power in respect of the stock we have guaranteed or taken over we would really control the Grand Trunk railway. So, as far as that is concerned, the Grand Trunk should have very little to say, morally at any rate, if we take the position we do here to-day.
Does my hon. friend take the ground that if we get the majority control we should force the minority shareholders into an arbitration into which they do not care to go?
No, I merely say that we are in equity more interested in the company than they are.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This agreement, if
acquiesced in by the shareholders, will be acquiesced in by those who remain, the preference and common.
At Six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
Consideration of Bill No. 80 respecting the Grand Trunk Arbitration resumed in Committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the Committee rose at six o'clock we had under consideration clause 1 of this Bill. Shall clause 1 carry.

Before this clause passes I would like to get a little information from the Prime Minister. With reference to sub-section (b) of clause 1, is the Grand Trunk Company still a corporate entity, and has it the power to hold meetings and appoint directors?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, it has.
It has all the functions of a joint stock company?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It has all the functions given to it under its charter, subject only to the provisions of the agreement and the Act ratifying the agreement.

I notice that the Government undertake to appoint directors under the authority of Parliament, and its truck me that, as the Grand Trunk Company is still a corpora-

tion with power to manage its own affairs and appoint directors, it might appoint a board and it would be a very intricate legal question as to which board of directors would have the necessary legal rights. The government undertakes to appoint a board and to say that this board shall not pay any attention to the shareholders and shall not take any instructions from them. The shareholders cannot dismiss the board the Government is going to appoint under this Bill, but cannot the Grand Trunk appoint a board of directors and have the legal right to do so?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There can be only one board of directors of the Grand Trunk Railway Company under its charter. Now there is a present board. By the contemplated agreement if it is made, the company will be compelled to have its present directors retire one by one, the remaining directors appointing a nominee of the Government. It is not strictly correct to say that the Government is to appoint anyone as a director. It does not. But the remaining directors are to appoint a nominee of the Government as a director in place of a man who resigns. That done, another man resigns and the directors appoint a nominee of the Government to the vacancy created. That done, another resigns and the directors appoint a nominee of the Government to the vacancy until the directorate is composed solely of nominees of the Government appointed by the board of directors.
Suppose they do net resign?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If they do not resign they cannot get the arbitration on. That is made a condition; that is the method of getting possession.
The terms of the agreement are stated in these sub-sections. May I ask if these terms have been submitted to the Grand Trunk representatives and if they are acceptable to them?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, they have not. Just prior to April 9, there were some discussions as to the carrying out of the Government's conditions that are now reduced to legal phraseology and embodied in the Bill. I could not say that they are just precisely as embodied therein, but, in general, the method of getting possession is. Nothing came of these discussions; the Grand Trunk was quite independent, and the consequence was that nothing was done.
Mr. Phippen and Mr. Kelley went over to England but there has been no further communication since. We ask Parliament to authorize the submission of these terms to the Grand Trunk and it is for that company to say whether it will accept them or not.
They must either take them wholesale or refuse to take them at all? No negotiations can be carried on to make them acceptable to. the Grand Trunk staff?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, I explained that in the statement I made on Tuesday last. We do not feel that it is any longer proper to approach them for negotiations. We think the time has come to say what we are ready to do and what we are not ready to do, feeling certain that all we lay before them is only fair and right.

With regard to subsection
(e) of the Bill, in the present state of feeling of the shareholders it is quite possible that they might not appoint a committee. If they do not appoint that committee can there not be provision made, by the Government or some one else, for deductions to pay their share of the costs of the arbitration?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think what the hon. member has in mind is that in case the Grand Trunk does not accept this Bill at all there will be no committee under subclause (e), and in that event there should be some provision made for deducting the costs already incurred, and there will be costs incurred, of course. No, I think the old Bill will take care of that, or rather the old agreement. The Government would be justified, as I understand the agreement, in deducting from the guaranteed shareholders' dividends any costs that remain unpaid or that are already charged against the Grand Trunk.

So far that is good. I
have in my mind another possibility, that perhaps under section 2, when we come to it, it would be possible that the company and the Government would come to an agreement and yet the shareholders stand aloof, in which case, again there should be some provision for the costs subsequently to be incurred because it is possible that the Government might accept their arrangement under clause 2 and go on. The other point as to costs is a small detail afer all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The company itself makes the arrangement with the Govern-

ment-that is if the company accepts these terms they enter into an agreement. That agreement would, I presume, be ratified by the shareholders. If the directors agreed to them, a meeting of shareholders would be called to ratify the agreement; time is given for that. Well, if the shareholders ratified the agreement it does not stand to reason that they would refuse to appoint a committee to look after their own interests. I do not think there is any chance of that. If they ratify this agreement they are going to appoint a committee to see that their interests are looked after in the arbitration.

In their present temper
that is just what they might not do.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Then they would have to take the consequences; I do not think we would suffer at all.

I would like to understand the situation in connection with this agreement which we have already made and which was duly executed. Is it not a fact that the necessary steps to complete the sale and transfer of the road to the Government hinge upon compliance with the terms of that agreement? Is it not necessary that to complete the agreement and its purpose both parties must comply with all the terms of the agreement? Now if one of the parties to the agreement refuses to comply with its terms, does not that give the other side the option of hacking out altogether if they want to? In view of the default of the Grand Trunk to comply with the terms under which the Government agreed to take over the road, does not that leave it open to.the Government to back out if they want to, or take the other steps which the Government seems to be taking now? I am not expressing an opinion, because I have not read that agreement, but as a rule if one party to an agreement defaults it leaves quite a number of options to the other party. For instance, he might sue for specific performance of the agreement, or he could back out and sue in damages. Those are the common law rights of parties to an agreement. _ I was trying to understand the real situation of the Government under the agreement when the Grand Trunk defaulted, as I understand it has, in this connection.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I will try to put my views before the hon. member, and I am sure he will not have much difficulty in following me, because he has already a pretty good grasp of the subject. For
[Mr* Meighen.]
some time I have been more or less living with this subject in its legal as well as every other aspect. Yes, if there are two parties to an executory agreement, and one defaults, at common law there is the right in the other to elect to abandon the agreement. But is that the case here? There are two parties to this agreement. It cannot be said that either has defaulted in such a way as to enable the other to elect to declare the agreement at an end. What is the default? There is no default on the part of the Government, that is certain. Now, as to the company; how could we establish that strictly they have defaulted, using that word in its legal sense? They have not finished their case. They did not bind themselves to finish their case. All the agreement said was:	You will have
nine months to complete the arbitration, or such further time as the Governor in Council may approve. They did not bind themselves and say: We will absolutely finish our case in nine months, and if we fail to do it, it is default vitiating the agreement. The hon. member will see at once that there is no such default as would vitiate the agreement. But the purpose of the agreement, namely, a final award, not having been reached in nine months, the agrement in that case lapses because there is no power in the arbitration board to make a finding. In that respect it is clear to the hon. member that there can be no final award. The Grand Trunk maintain: Even though that is the result, you have to pay the dividends on the debenture and guaranteed stock, because that was a condition precedent to our giving up our voting power, and so forth. It is contended on the other side, that the whole agreement is one

that if they cannot carry out one part, none can be carried out.
I would not like to express an opinion which of those two views is right, nor do I think it important. Because, as was frankly stated two years ago, there is no disposition whatever on the part of the Government to seek to escape their responsibility provided we get the system. We are quite ready as well, if there is any value in the rest of the stock, to pay the fair value that may be found by the arbitrators. That question does not arise. I really do not like to give legal opinions in this way, but I do so now for just what they are worth. I do not think anything has occurred which could be described as default of such a character as would enable the Government to elect to consider the whole thing at an end.
All I have to say to my right hon. friend is that it is a most novel situation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Most situations are.
Well, this is a most extraordinary situation. I am not saying that by way of criticism. In a very long and extensive practice I never came across a case where default of this kind has arisen.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Is it default?

If it is not default, what is it? It is non-compliance with the terms of the contract. Whose fault it is I do not know, and I am not expressing any opinion. But the terms were that within a certain limit of time conditions precedent to the taking over of the road were to be complied with. I understand there was a proviso in the agreement for extension of the time for the arbitration. The most extraordinary thing is that the company did not apply for any extension. Did the arbitrators have power to extend the time?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not without the approval of the Government.
Was application made for an extension of the time?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not think any formal application was made. The hon. member will see in one of Sir Alfred Smithers' cablegrams, dated about March 23, that the Grand Trunk directors wanted an extension of three months. But the power remained in the Government to agree or disagree, and if the Government did not agree there could not be any extension, and the arbitration closed. I think it is manifest that inasmuch as the Government had to give its approval to an extension, in giving that approval the Government had to decide whether or not it was in the public interest to give it; and if there should be conditions attached, what, having regard to all the circumstances that had developed in the meantime, those conditions should be.

I would remind the minister in charge that when this matter came before the committee originally in 1919 it was pointed out to the present Prime Minister that the agreement was being made between the majority shareholders -who were being guaranteed their interest in any event-and the Government of Canada. The majority shareholders, or the
guaranteed shareholders, then undertook to arbitrate the value of the minority shareholders' stock. Now I think that is where the difficulty arises with regard to the arbitration. I do not think there is any question about the majority shareholders opposing or delaying this arbitration in any way. Apparently the whole difficulty arises with the minority shareholders, who are the people affected by this arrangement. The majority shareholders are now in a better position than they were before, and better than they can be if the agreement is not carried out. So apparently a deal was made between the Government and Smithers to guarantee certain stocks, provided that the Grand Trunk people would agree to arbitrate the balance. The minority ' shareholders have apparently never been quite satisfied with this arrangement, and the position now appears to be that the Government are not quite prepared to say whether these minority shareholders are the only people with whom they will have to deal. The majority shareholders, or the debenture holders, will of course be ifi the majority as the member for North Grey mentioned this evening.
By the agreement they are not shareholders at all now.

Just exactly. That gets us to the point where two people who are not interested in this undertaking for their own selfish ends are undertaking to arbitrate some other persons' stock. That is the point I put to the hon. member for Grey this afternoon. The Government and the majority shareholders, who are in no way interested in this undertaking, are attempting to arbitrate the value of certain stock of the minority stockholders, and the latter are the people who are objecting. Now we propose to pass legislation that will further curtail their rights in this matter, if they have any. I do not claim that they have any value in their stock; I do not believe they have-the minister's argument this afternoon -would rather lead me to believe that. But that is the stock we are undertaking to arbitrate; that is the stock we are legislating on now. There is no question about the majority shareholders, the people who have their stocks guaranteed.

My hon. friend continually refers to the majority shareholders. He should remember that there are no majority shareholders now; their Votes

have been wiped out. The only shareholders now are shareholders other than those who formerly had voting powers on the guaranteed and debenture stocks.
I would ask the Prime Minister if that is his understanding of it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is true. I must say, though, that I do not think it affects the point my hon. friend is trying to make, because they had votes when the original agreement was made. My hon. friend's point is that having votes then, they virtually entered into a bargain, as he says, with the Government to arbitrate the value of the shares of the minority. In a way, that is correct. It turns out that the guananteed and debenture stockholders had the majority at the time of the making of the first agreement. But they have not now any voting power; they were compelled under the agreement to give up all control. So that when this agreement goes before them they will have nothing to say about it; it will be only for those holding the preference and common stock. The hon. member is quite wrong if he believes that Sir Alfred Smitners made an arrangement thoroughly satisfactory to him and not at all to the holders of the preference and common stock. I did not come in contact with the holders of the preference and common stock, but if there is any worse state of dissatisfaction than that on the part of Sir Alfred Smithers, I would be sorry for the fact. He is by no means elated at the arrangement made or at the position of things to-day. The Government could not make an arrangement with any except the majority; there was no other way to do it. We could not say: We will deal only with the minority; we had to deal with the whole of them.

That is not the point. You took certain stocks that were not guaranteed or debenture stocks, selected enough of them to make a majority to support your contention, took them out of one class, put them Jnto another, and gave them preference rights over the minority stock holders.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, we did not give them any preference rights at all. They had those rights before.
They had no guarantee before except the guarantee of the common stock and the preferred stock.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
But they had a prior claim on the earnings of the company. They

were in a position of first mortgagees. It was just a case of the mortgages having
votes in the running of the concern, as well as the owners of the equity of redemption. The Government was faced with the necessity of dealing with all the shareholders. It all became a question of whether we were to meet the request that we assume what you might describe as the mortgage on the property. That we did. I know it is open to the criticism that the majority, being, as they were, secured, would perhaps vote from their own point of view rather than from the point of view of the. company. But that was inherent in the whole situation; you could not avoid that. I think it is a fact-I do not want to say this with finality, al-thought I can verify it-that the majority of the preference and common stockholders, did vote for the transaction. They wanted to carry it through, and it is only natural that they would. They knew we had a lot to fear from liquidation and they knew they would get nothing, so it is only natural they would vote for it. They were not done any injustice, that is certain. They are not being done any injustice now-that is if I know what injustice is.
Who will vote the debenture stock at the proposed meeting to ratify?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Nobody. It has no ratifying power at all.

It must have voting power.
M^. MEIGHEN: No there is no voting power except in the preference and common. It will go entirely before the holders of those stocks.

So this agreement now
being presented to the shareholders will go only before the first preference, second preference, third preference and the ordinary stockholders.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is right.

Those are the stocks
that are to be arbitrated?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

The holders of these
stocks will finally decide, then, whether or not they will accept this agreement?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is right.

If they refuse to accept
it, what position will the Government find themselves in? Are the Government bound then on the other stocks?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Well, they claim so.
We have not admitted it. We take the stand, and have always taken it, that, bound or not bound-we do not seek to evade our obligations-it will be for us to see that we get the property at that price or on such terms as may appeal to Parliament as right. It will be for us to consider, if they do not accept this, what the next step should be. I do not fear at all that it will not be in our power in some way to see that the end we have sought from the beginning is achieved or that we shall not be able to protect ourselves. Our anxiety is to do so in such a way that Canadians of this generation and future generations will not have to look back to the transaction and say that we were unfair to anybody.

Unless it would be to
the Canadian people.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: To either.

The member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) this afternoon was giving us a great deal of what he thought to be enlightenment on the subject of bondholders. But there are no such things in this transaction as bondholders. The securities in this case are all debenture stocks-first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth and seventh preference stocks. There are no bondholders. The Government make the claim that there is about $250,000,000 worth of equity in these debentures which are the property of the Grand Trunk shareholders. My hon. friend's argument with regard to the receivership falls to the ground, because the Government maintain that there is $250,000,000 worth of equity there before the subsidiary companies are touched. You have that to come and go on, as it were. If a receiver were appointed, these debenture holders would have to find a way of financing the road for the present and getting themselves out of their difficulties. The Prime Minister told us to-day that they were earning sufficient to pay their operating charges, so' that after all the only think they are short of, apparently, is the interest on these debentures, and they are not going to throw away these debentures because they do not receive the interest on them. It is merely a matter for the debenture holders to decide whether they want to wait or not. But instead of that the Government step in and say:	All
right, we will pay you interest on this, we will undertake this whole transaction. What for? Because, they say, we require this system as a feeder for the National
Railways. Now, "feeder" is not the proper word to use. It will cost more money to maintain the Canadian National Railway system with the Grand Trunk than without it, so that it is something to be fed rather than a feeder. According to what evidence we can get, it will cost us this year in the neighbourhood of $25,000,000 to $50,000,000 to maintain the road. There was an item last year of $25,000,000; I do not know whether the loan was made or not. But we also made loans to the Canadian National, and the Minister of Finance tells us that they are not such as he considers as live assets,

in other words, that it is lost money. We have $70,000,000 deficit on our National railways, and thirty, forty or fifty million dollars more on the Grand Trunk. Why the haste in getting into this further deficit on the railways? We have deficits enough now. If we leave the Grand Trunk alone to work out their own salvation, we shall be saving this country an expenditure of $25,000,000 to $50,000,000 a year for the next ten years, so that we might just as well let the Grand Trunk work this out themselves. My hon. friend says that we must get the system to round out the National system. The same result can be achieved by co-operation. The Grand Trunk will give the Canadian National system an interchange of traffic arrangement which will lead to absolutely the same advantage that the Government have if they take the road over, with this difference that the Grand Trunk people will finance themselves instead of the country financing them and paying out from twentv-five to fifty millions a year.
As regards the question of receivership, my hon. friends are getting scared before they come to the difficulty. No difficulty would arise. The present debenture holders would take care of the matter themselves. Hon. gentlemen opposite tell us in one breath that the debenture holders are unable to do that. They tell us in the next that they are able to do it. There is absolutely no sense in that argument. Let the bondholders try it out. If the Grand Trunk goes into the hands of a receiver and the receiver finally comes to the point where he is to sell the road, the Government can gain possession of the road, with this difference that they will save several hundred millions of dollars to the Canadian people. After all, our business is to look after the interests of the Canadian people and not after the interests of shareholders or debenture holders of some (railroad. That is their business. The Government

should bear in mind that our duty is to look after the interests of the Canadian people instead of trying to furnish money to some persons, because we think we need something which the majority of the people of this country are absolutely satisfied we do not need.

I should like to know if my hon. friend is proposing that the Canadian people should cancel a debt which the Grand Trunk owe us in regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific. He said that there would not be a receivership unless the debenture holders took action. The only way to avoid a receivership is for the Canadian people to cancel the debt which the Grand Trunk owe us on the Grand Trunk Pacific.

Would it not be very much better for the Canadian people to forego the interest on their investment in the Grand Trunk Pacific amounting to some eight or ten million dollars than to undertake an expenditure of forty or fifty million dollars a year? The question is one of saving what you can. We are getting into the hole further all the time. My hon. friend surely would not contend that it is good business, in order to save the first ten million dollars, to take over the Grand Trunk at a cost of forty or fifty million dollars a year. It is not necessary to take any action at all. If the only difficulty that confronts us is the matter of the interest on our investments in the Grand Trunk Pacific, why not let the Grand Trunk go ahead with their enterprise, because every time we get into a new railway enterprise, we are only adding that much more by way of deficit and taxation to the burdens of the Canadian people?

Unless we have the
Grand Trunk in the East, the Grand Trunk Pacific in the West would not be of very much use. As was stated by the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), we would have the Grand Trunk Pacific with one end in the air, with no eastern connections for it, because the Grand Trunk Pacific was built as a western connection for the Grand Trunk.

I pointed out just a few moments ago that the Grand Trunk were in the same position. They have no western outlet. What are they going to do? They naturally will make a traffic arrangement with the people who have a western outlet. They have an eastern line; we have a western line; they will make a traffic arrangement that will suit both parties and 
that will be much more satisfactory than this business of taking over the Grand Trunk and running it at a cost to the Canadian people of forty or fifty million dollars a year.

The Grand Trunk
would like exactly what my hon. friend proposes, namely, that the (Government cancel the interest which they owe in regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific. That is not what the Government of Canada is apparently willing to do, and personally, I think the Government is upholding the rights of the Canadian people much more by insisting on having that debt paid.

On having the debt paid with their own money! That is the most nonsensical argument in the world. The Government are not getting any money from outside; they are putting more money into this enterprise.

They are getting the
Grand Trunk.

They are paying not only the debt, but three times the debt in order to pay it. The Government are not getting any money from any outside source; they are taking over another defunct proposition and paying a huge price for it. What for? My hon. friend from Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) says, "to save expenditures already made," and he is going to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to protect something that is already lost. Would it not be better for the Canadian people to take their first loss and be done with it, than to pile on millions more and to have deficits piling up year after year? The Government apparently are getting in worse on the Canadian National, and they will continue to get in worse with the Grand Trunk attached to it. To take over the Grand Trunk is only adding to the difficulties.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 2-agreement to revive and continue arbitration proceedings to be made on or before May 16, 1921.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Was the committee of management of five . ever appointed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What has
become of it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is still there.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What will become of it if this passes?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
By subclause (b) of clause 1, one of the things that must be provided for if there an extension is:
That the directors of the company appointed upon the nomination of the Government as aforesaid, in addition to their other powers, shall have and may exercise all the powers and functions of the committee of management as provided by the said agreement.
That is to say, the committee of management ceases, and the new board has all the powers the committee of management had, as well as the regular powers of the company.

This afternoon my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen). answered an inquiry regarding the right of appeal. I understand, under this clause, that my right hon. friend has no apprehension as to the continuance of the right of appeal because of his taking over control and management of the road. As I understand the matter, the right of appeal still inures under the new agreement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is undoubtedly
the intention. We do not intend to take away any right which the Grand Trunk would have under the old agreement.
Before the arbitration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes. I know that is not the intention of the draughtsmen. I know that Mr. Newcombe and Mr. Tilley have no intention of taking away the right of appeal. I will draw their attention to my hon. friend's apprehension.
I simply wanted to be satisfied that, in my right hon. friend's mind, there is no doubt as to the right of appeal being continued. I do not raise any doubt as to the drafting of the clause.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I know there is no
intention that the right of appeal shall be taken away. The intention is that the right shall remain.
Was the date, May 16, arrived at for any particular reason?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
One is that we knew that the Bill would be introduced last Tuesday, and we thought we would get on a little more rapidly, but perhaps we have got on as rapidly as is well. The company's by-laws require two weeks' notice in the Canada Gazette before they can call a meeting of the shareholders. It would take some days to arrange for the meeting, and
then it should be held a little while before that date. I thought that when they knew the terms that the Government were willing to give, there was nothing to hinder them from calling a meeting of shareholders, and they could give sufficient notice of the purpose of it to enable them to decide at the meeting, and by the time they met, the agreement could be all ready. We thought May 16 would give them sufficient time to do that. I hope it will yet.

They cannot lawfully
proceed to give notice until this Bill becomes law, can they?/

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I think so.

A notice given in
anticipation of this would not be in compliance with the Act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think they could give notice in this way. A special meeting of the shareholders could be called for the purpose of authorizing the directors to enter into an agreement for the continuation of the arbitration. As long as the subject matter of the meeting were given in the notice, I think that would be sufficient.
They can, but will they? And if they do not, will the time be sufficient?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If they do not, it will not be sufficient.
Would it not be better, then, to extend the time? I am only suggesting that to save time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is just possible we
might have to come and ask Parliament for a short extension, but we do not want to do that if we can help it.

It is only a few days
since the Bill was introduced, and I think it would be nothing but reasonable to give them at least a month, and make it the 25th instead of the 16th. It would be better to do that now, than to have to come and ask Parliament for an extension.

These large bodies .
move slowly, and especially a body the greater part of which is over in England and the officials here. I can easily imagine there may be many difficulties in calling a meeting so promptly. That is all I care to bring to the attention of the right hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Large bodies move
slowly, and I hope I will be forgiven if 1 say, especially this large body.
That makes my point the stronger.

That is why we want
to extend the time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I considered the question yesterday and to-day as to whether or not before this goes through committee we should add a few days to it, but I rather came to the conclusion that if we found that was absolutely necessary it might be done in the Senate. I think we will know to-morrow definitely whether or not it will be absolutely necessary. I am getting details as to just the amount of time that will be required. My own opinion is that it would be better to have it go through the way it is.

If you want to make
a show of fairness in all these things, and I am sure we want to make even more than a show of fairness, it would look better not to crowd them for time in connection with this meeting.

I think the question of
extending this period for a week or ten days, or even two weeks, is not of great moment, if it will avoid unfavourable criticism on the part of the shareholders. We are taking pretty strong action, although, as I expressed myself this afternoon, I do not know there is very much else for the Government to do, but I think it would be well to be as fair in this matter as it is possible for us to be.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is quite right,
but I want to lay this point clearly before the committee. If this time is extended, say even a week, that brings us to May 23. Now we may not know until pretty nearly say even a week, that brings us to the that time whether they are going to agree or not. We may not know for some time.
I have not the least doubt myself that if they do not agree there will .
9 p.m. be further legislation necessary to be considered by Parliament, and very important legislation, and the hon. member will see how far in the session that would be. We do not want to find ourselves in the position of having to come to Parliament right at the end of the session with' very important legislation, if we can avoid it. We would like to have as much time for consideration as possible. At the same time, the necessity of being reasonable, and" of not forcing the day too hard, is great, and I suggest this: if we pass this to-day, it is quite probable that the Senate will be able to deal with it on Monday or Tuesday, and

I am in hopes that before that time we will have details as to whether a few days more will be necessary or not. I could intimate to the leader of the Senate whether they were or not, and have the extension made there if it was vital that a few days more should be added, and then the Bill could come back here.
