I would not like to add a single day unless it were absolutely necessary.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 3-powers and duties of arbitrators to continue if Governor in Council extend time:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I would ask my right hon. friend if he would not reconsider the matter of submitting this agreement to Parliament when it is drafted. He may recall that at the time the arrangement was first entered into, it was suggested on this side of the House that the agreement should be submitted to Parliament. My right hon. friend refused that, but he came back the next year and submitted the agreement for ratification. He might save a repeated action of the kind if he took the step of submitting the agreement to Parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member does not state why it was that we came back last year with the agreement.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There were errors.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
But not any errors of ours. The Grand Trunk in sending out the notice omitted sending notice to certain debenture holders, I think it was; at all events, to some shareholders. The company had the notice put in the Canada Gazette all right, but in the letters, which many lawyers thought it was not necessary for it to send at all, certain classes of shareholders were omitted through an error, and therefore there arose a doubt as to the validity of the ratification on the company's part. The only body which could make it good in any event was this House. It was not an error of the Government in any way; it was the company's error. The Grand Trunk also in giving us a schedule of their subsidiary properties omitted two subsidiary companies. That also made it necessary to have the agreement submitted to Parliament. The errors were entirely the company's. There was no error on our part. As to submitting this agreement to Parliament, how could we say to the Grand Trunk: Here are our terms; take

them or leave them; if you leave them all right, but if you take them we want them to come back here and we want to think them over again? I cannot see how you could logically take that position at all. To go to the Grand Trunk and say definitely: Here are the terms upon which we will resuscitate this arbitration; now it is for you to elect; if the company elects "yes," how can we say then, we want to have this considered over again? It would be rather humiliating.

That is not the point. The power to make an agreement stipulated in an Act of Parliament, and the agreement itself, are two different things. They are never exactly the same. The draftsman who draws up the agreement uses his own language, and the wording is never the same as in the Act. All we ask is that when you put it into shape we would like to look at your agreement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We will grant the hon. gentleman that right.
As a Parliament, I mean. I am not so dull as my right hon. friend may suppose.

Is it contemplated that the term of the extension should be at the discretion of the Government? The Bill does not say the arbitration may be extended for a given time. It is practically an unlimited power of extension, if I read it aright.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We wish to have control of it, so the Grand Trunk cannot get it extended indefinitely while we have our railway engineers and all the rest of our witnesses under pay. We do not want to be in that position, but we do not like to fix here a definite period and say: We will only give you that long anyway. We do not want the shareholders to be able to say: The Government not only took over our road and went into possession, but after it was in possession, would only allow us so long to finish the arbitration.
They were only allowed a limited time before?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, I know, but the Grand Trunk were in possession; and there was power of extension on the part of the Government then. We shall now have the same power, and I cannot think of any state of affairs that would warrant us in refusing extension, except the clearest pos-
157i
sible evidence that the company was delaying for the sake of delay.

Instead of leaving the date to be fixed, would it not be advisable, in the interests both of the public and of Parliament, to provide that the arbitration shall be concluded and the award made, not later than a certain date?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is really what is provided now; the arbitration is subject to extension. [DOT]
Why not fix it so that there will be no extension beyond a given time?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That would not leave it in our hands; you would have to fix a definite time, and that would be wholly unreasonable. The question of extension had better be left in the hands of the Government.
As to length of time?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think so.

What is the significance of the word "further" in the first clause? The clause provides that terms may be made upon which the Governor in Council "may approve of a further time," etc. What does that word "further" signify?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In the first clause the recital refers to the time which they had previously; then the Governor in Council "may approve of a further time." Clause 3 refers to the aproval by the Governor in Council "of a further time," which is the time provided in clause 1.
Will the new agreement provide that all the shares shall be turned over before the money which may be payable under the award is paid?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, and that is inherent in the old agreement. In the old agreement the shareholders could not get anything on account of the award until they turned in the stock, because it was only on the turning in of the stock that the new guaranteed stock issued in pursuance of the award. The award was made payable in new guaranteed stock, and that was to be given only when the old stock was turned in.	,
Will the agreement provide that no award shall be made unless the shareholders turn in the stock?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. The terms of the old agreement are revived in that respect,

and when the award is made they can get nothing unless they turn in the old stock. We should be just that much better off if they did not turn in the old stock, because we should not have to pay dividends.

The stock arrangement is different now from what it was previously. The ordinary stock now will have practically 50 per cent of voting power, and in my judgment that stock will not be entitled to any dividend under this arbitration. Now, if the common stockholders say they will not give up their stock, what position will the Government be in?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This will be the position: The Government's directors will be running the road in full control, able to do everything that directors can do, as the hon. member will see if he will read paragraphs (b) and (d). So that the common stockholders could not have any say whatever in the running of the system; they could not get any dividends because dividends would be no longer payable, and the stockholders would simply stay out enjoying the dignity of being old shareholders of the Grand Trunk. I cannot see what other advantage they would have. Furthermore, the Government takes power under the legislation to declare that stock, if the shareholders do not turn it in, the property of the Government, and to issue in its stead guaranteed stock, if there is any coming to them under the award. Of course, if they are entitled to none, ngne will be issued. But even if that power were not exercised, I do not see that there is any element in the situation that would be embarrassing to the Government. If the shareholders want to remain outside in possession of their certificates, I do not think it will hurt the management of the road.

The Prime Minister will not argue that we can take possession of stock outside of this country. We might legislate in that way in regard to stocks held in Canada, but this stock is held outside of Canada. It follows that if you paid dividends on all the debenture stock and the preferred stock, and there were a surplus, the common stockholders would be entitled to it. I do not see how the Government can take possession of stock outside of Canada by legislation in this country, if the shareholders refuse to give it up. As a matter of fact, as I see the situation, the common stockholders would be the owners of the road, and I do not see how you can take possession of their stock.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Government is advised that this stock is Canadian property. Even though its owners may live in England, even though the paper that represents it may lie in England, the stock is stock of a Canadian company chartered by this country. That being the case, the Government is advised that that stock may be expropriated and declared the property of the Government of Canada by this Parliament. Now, even if there may be doubt about that, even if there are others who might think differently from the legal standpoint, the only contingency one can imagine, in which there would be any embarrassment to the Government, would be this, that the common stockholders might stand by and not hand in their stock, because they get nothing under the award, and theii claim later on to be shareholders of the company. They cannot vote; that is clear, because the Bill provides that the company shall agree that our directors shall go in and stay in, not subject at all to the vote of the stockholders. Under the old agreement, which is revived, they agreed, as well, that they would hand in their stock, and they cannot get a dividend from the concern until they do. So that all that I can see they could ever hope to gain would be the pleasure of having the certificates in their vaults.

Where is the head office
of the company?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The head office is now
in London, under the charter of the company.

Is there any legislation
changing its location?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, but this legislation provides that they may meet in Canada.

Well, the , head office
being in London, if the shareholders refuse to give up their stock they can hold their meetings there, which is the legal place. The Government would have no voting power there, and the shareholders might continue, and some day, if the road became valuable, you would have a lawsuit on your hands. Before the agreement is concluded you had better provide against such a contingency; make arrangements to get the stock before anything further is done, or there will be difficulty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Government is
doing precisely that now. The Government is going to these common share-

holders and to the preference shareholders and saying, "Are you ready to do this? Are you ready to agree to do this?" And they agree to do it. What more can you do? You cannot follow them up and physically take it from them.
Mr. CAHILL; No, because they are outside the country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: You could not do it if they were here.
Yes, you could by legislation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That they happen to be outside the country does not affect the question. For example, if to-day we want a certain piece of property and the owner is in England our Expropriation Act applies just the same: we go and take it. It is Canadian property and subject to the jurisdiction of the proper legislative tribunal of this country, so we go and take it. The fact that the owner resides in London or Jericho does not matter in the least. As we are advised, it is the same in respect to the stock of a Canadian company. This is a Canadian company and the fact that its head office is in London or Paris does not make it any the less so, and its property is subject to the jurisdiction of the Canadian Parliament.
And the property is in Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, most of the property.
Some property, not all of it.

These legal points always interest me. I do not agree with the Prime Minister that a stock certificate can be confiscated by Parliament when it is held and owned by a man outside of Canada. I may be wrong, but that is my view of the law. That is property in itself. There is property in that stock certificate which he holds; it is transferable and negotiable, and the owner can sell it, in whatever method is provided, by endorsing it and passing it over. It is like a dollar note. If we in Canada issue a dollar bill it is, in a way, Canadian property. These Government bills are Canadian property and they are redeemable by the Government, but they are negotiable and they are currency. Suppose that dollar bill gets into the hands of a man who is here from Paris and he goes home with it in his pocket. Of course the origin of that property is in Canada and it has, the guarantee of this country, but the dollar passes from hand to hand in Europe. Does my right hon. friend mean that we can deprive the man who holds that dollar bill of its validity and of its intrinsic value by some legislation in this House? I do not think so. I do not want the Prime Minister to answer me at all. I am simply making my view clear that my opinion is-and it is given for what it is worth-that there is intrinsic value in the stock certificate. It is property in the possession of the owner. It is negotiable- and we cannot constitutionally interfere with it in this country when the property owner, the man who owns it, is not within our jurisdiction.
Is stock negotiable like a dollar bill?
Debentures are; they are transferable.
Transferable but not negotiable.

I think it is a very nice distinction to make. I do not see much difference between "transferability and negotiability". There may be to the mind of the hon. gentleman but not to a blunt Scotchman like myself.
Bill reported.
On motion of Mr. Meighen that the Bill be read a third time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I think it is only proper to point out that practically all the legislation pertaining to the Grand Trunk railway has been railroaded through Parliament. The very first Bill for the acquisition of this road was introduced at the eleventh hour and rushed through in great haste. When the Bill to confirm the agreement was brought into the House we were told it must be confirmed within two or three days. Now we get the present Bill brought in on two or three days' notice and the Prime Minister wishes to rush it through to-night. I think opportunity should be given to the people of the country as well as to the members of the House to understand this legislation. We ought also to have the benefit of the opinions of the press and of the public to guide Parliament as well as the views of hon. members.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I understand we have the right to ask for the third reading of the Bill and I would like very much to have

it to take place. I will give reasons for my desire. I must say that if the Bill has been railroaded through, even though it is a railroad Bill, I do not know just what the process of railroading has been; I do not hold either end of the steel. We have tried to have the measure considered at as early a date as possible-that is true,-but for the most obvious reasons and in order to avoid, if possible, having to bring in legislation at the end of the session. For myself, I have not very much objection to that method but there is always complaint to bringing in anything at the end of the session except when it is a case of adjourning. I do not know how you could get to the end of the session without doing some work. It is in order to avoid having to bring in legislation at the end of the session, to which hon. gentlemen opposite object, that I desired to get this Bill considered as speedily by the House as was fair and reasonable. If we wait until Monday Public Bills and Orders may not be called-it is private members' day.
The list is very short though. I think my right hon. friend will be able to proceed with the third reading then.
I would like to remind the Prime Minister that there was an amendment proposed by the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy), which he promised to consider.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, and I did.
Then you are not entitled to read your Bill if there was an amendment made to it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not think that because an amendment is considered we cannot read a Bill.
Not a third time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I had the amendment carefully considered by the Deputy Minister of Justice and his opinion was that the amendment was not necessary because the word " nominated, " used in subclause (b) of clause 1 is right-for the reason that the Government only nominates directors; it does not appoint them. The word " appoint " could not be used because the Government only nominates tho directors and they are appointed by the other directors-that is the reason. As to paragraph (c) the language employed there " Board of Directors " is right-it should be the board. The horn member for

Neepawa suggested that the word " duly " be omitted from clause (a). It is not necessary but the deputy minister thinks it is rather better in that it merely provides that the appointing shall be done as it should be done by the appointing body.

I certainly think the Government in rushing this Bill through in
the manner which is proposed is not creating a favourable impression either here or in England. It is a very important measure and reasonable notice of it should be given. My hon. friend is open to some criticism in the matter; he brought down essential correspondence that was not printed. In a matter of such great importance correspondence should be laid on the Table in printed form. As a matter of fact an important section of that correspondence was not submitted at all, and it was not until the discussion this afternoon that we succeeded in getting the letter. These are evidences of rushing this legislation through, and whether my hon. friend means it or not, it is creating a bad impression on the part of the country and interested parties abroad. I do not think it is a wise policy to (rush through legislation of such importance in such a very short time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The only letter that was not brought down was received after we had tabled the correspondence. I read it to-day. It will be seen that it could not affect the merits of this legislation.
That is a matter of opinion; others might differ.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think the Government has been pretty frank with Parliament in this matter. The custom would be to bring down the correspondence when the Bill was introduced, but we brought the correspondence down two weeks ahead of the usual time. However, as for the third reading, this is an important Bill, and I know that hon. gentlemen opposite feel the responsibility of carrying this matter along until perhaps we 'may be under the necessity of holding Parliament longer and the responsibility is shared generally. But under the circumstances I will agree that the third reading be not dealt with now. But I would bespeak this consideration that on Monday there be no objection-even though we do not reach it-to the third reading being taken up.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Third reading, next sitting of the House.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On the motion of Hon. J. A. Calder (President of the Privy Council) Bill No. 82, to amend the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act, was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-fines and forfeitures earned by members of the force to be paid to the Minister; how money to be used; regulations:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Will the minister explain what is meant by this amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
As I explained on the first reading, there is a feeling that this practice, which has been followed for some years, should be put an end to because it is considered that the results are not at all conducive to building up the proper morale and spirit of the force itself. There are some four federal statutes under which in cases where mounted policemen are the informers, and the parties are found guilty and fined, the informers are entitled to a portion of the fines. There has been a good deal of feeling in the force with reference to that. The chief officers think that the practice is a very bad one, and that while those provisions should remain in the law, nevertheless the moneys paid in that way should be set apart as a special fund to be used for the benefit of the members of the force and their families. After making inquiries I have been unable to ascertain the amounts that have been paid to individual members of the force under the four federal statutes, namely the Inland Revenue Act, the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, the Indian Act and the Customs Act, because when convictions are obtained against offenders the magistrate simply orders that a portion of the fine be paid over to the informant. From all that I have been able to gather in the discussions I have had with officers of the force, I find that they are of opinion that this practice should cease.
As regards the matter of pensions, from inquiry I made this afternoon I find that a man must be in the force for ten years before he is entitled to a pension. Occasionally a man retires from the force because of ill health or something of that kind before he has completed the ten years' service, and it is felt that if a benefit fund of this character were established, those moneys might very well be used to assist
members of the force so retiring. That, of course, would only he in deserving cases.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I find some difficulty in reconciling a couple of statements made by the hon. gentleman. In explanation of the reasons for introducing this amendment , my hon. friend said that the practice had given rise to considerable dissatisfaction among members of the force.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Not among the men.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Then among whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It is felt that this practice does not conduce to building up the proper spirit and morale of the force itself. If a mounted policeman, or in fact any policeman, has evidence he should lay his information without looking forward to receiving any portion of the penalty. I dare say the men who happen to receive portions of these fines will not complain, but, on the other hand, it is held that there will be a better feeling throughout the entire force if this practice is done away with.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Can the hon. gentleman say what amounts were distributed among members of the force by reason of their sharing in these fines?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
No. Probably if I had
more time I might be able to ascertain what amount has been received altogether, but I think it would require a good deal of searching to ascertain the amounts paid to individual members of the force.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Has the practice been
so extensive that it would take considerable staff and time to ascertain the amounts that have been distributed?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I imagine we would have to get in touch with every magistrate in the country.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Taking members of the
force who were here in Ottawa, would it not be possible to ascertain from them what fines they have shared in?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I imagine that could be
done fairly quickly.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Could the hon. gentleman do that before the Bill goes through?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has stated that application would have to be made to magistrates all over the country to ascertain what fines were imposed and what portions of those fines were distributed among members of the force. Is the hon. gentleman aware that there may have been

a distribution of moneys outside of that directed by magistrates?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I am not.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I might refer him to a
case here in Ottawa where a member of the force undertook to impose, and did in fact impose, a fine and collected it from the offender. Having done that it is-well, it is a safe assumption that no return of it was made either to a magistrate or to the superior officer of the force.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I doubt very much if the practice has prevailed at all. Unless a member of the mounted police force was a magistrate sitting on a case, he would have no right to impose a fine and put the proceeds in his own pocket. If the hon. gentleman has information with regard to any such case, I should like to have the particulars from him in order that I may follow them up and see just what the facts are.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I have information to that effect, and I shall be very glad to give it to the hon. gentleman. I will remind him of the matter a little later in case there is any dilatoriness in letting the House know the result of my supplying him with the information. I do not know whether the gentleman who acted as the arresting officer, the magistrate, and the recipient of the fine-he was a pooh bah on that occasion-is still a member of the force. If he is not, I am ready to admit that the hon. gentleman might not be able to pursue the inquiry very far. But it does seem to me that he ought to be able to give the committee more reasons than he has given for the introduction of this amendment. Surely there must be something before the department showing the necessity for such an amendment, and some, specific instances must have arisen. I think the committee is entitled to that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It seems to me that it does not make any difference whether ten mounted policemen received a fraction of the penalties, or twenty, or thirty, or fifty, or one hundred. There is a principle involved. The question is whether under the law the mounted policemen in the discharge of their duties should be entitled to a moiety of these fines. Personally I think they should not. This practice has been in force for a number of years, and most officers of the mounted police have also come to the conclusion that it should cease.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Will it be any better if we adopt the proposed amendment providing that the penalty shall go to some club or association?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Oh, yes, there is a great difference, because the individual interest is-eliminated. For instance, under the Opium and Narcotic Drug (Act, if a mounted policeman knows that if he follows up a certain case he will get a portion of the fine, he will probably be more interested in it than he otherwise would be. But if that portion goes into a fund for the benefit of members of the force and their families, he will look at the matter differently. What the chief officers of the mounted police desire to do is to create a feeling in the force that every man should do his full duty regardless of any fraction of a fine that should come to him. .

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is it not the practice to give to those securing convictions for violation of the customs regulations a portion of the fine imposed? I doubt whether it is very objectionable to give to officers of the law a portion of penalties in these cases. I am not quite sure that the judgment of the officers of the mounted police is based on human experience when they recommend the adoption of this amendment in preference to the present practice.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Do these sums paid to the mounted police not constitute practically an increase in pay, and when you deprive them of it, are you not, in effect, reducing their pay? I must say I like the principle laid down by the minister, but if these sums have been fairly widely distributed, one who has hitherto been in the habit of receiving them may feel that his pay is being reduced. You are cutting off a perquisite; it is like saying to a waiter: You shall get no tips, but there will be no increase in your salary.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Well, there is something in that.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am glad this matter has been brought up. I would like, if it were possible, to broaden the discussion on this Bill; I presume, though, it is not in order to discuss the matter generally. The practice which this Bill deals with is somewhat general in all branches of the Inland Revenue Department. I know personally of many cases where inspectors or officers of the Inland Revenue Department have stooped to very questionable methods in order to secure evidence to bring about a

conviction and thus obtain a share of the fine. My view is that officers intrusted with that work should be sufficiently well paid not to require any inducements of this kind. When these inducements are held out to them, they are apt to be overofficious; the effect is a degrading and a demoralizing influence upon the public service. I am sure that the Minister of Inland Revenue and the deputy minister of the department could furnish many instances wherein officers have exceeded what is required of them by the department and by the law in order to secure convictions and to get a portion of the fine. The whole principle has a demoralizing effect on the branch of the public service concerned and the practice should be entirely eliminated. If our police officers are not paid sufficiently without getting inducements or considerations of this kind, or without getting a bonus, commission or rake-off, then their salaries should be increased. No matter whether the portion of the fine is paid to an individual person or to an organization as provided in this . Bill, the principle is wrong, and should be done away with.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I take it that the object of assigning a portion of the fine to officers making arrests is to ensure greater diligence on the part of those officers. If that is now to be abolished the object disappears altogether. I quite agree with what the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) says; but I would go just a bit further than that, and I would say that no moiety of those fines should go anywhere except into the public treasury of the country or of the municipality,-into the funds of the Government, let us say. If the whole object was, in the first place, to ensure diligence, as I have said, why should this be continued by paying the money into an association? The thing is illogical; it ought to be abolished.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am not so certain but
that the idea of creating a benefit fund is a very good one. As a matter of fact, I know, from information that has come to me from time to time, that many of the old members of the force get into very serious financial difficulties. They have the Veterans' Association, and I am not so certain but that it would be advisable, if this Bill is passed, that provision he made under it for the payment of some grants to that Veterans' Association. Many members of the House are familiar with the work of that association and the burdens
that they have to carry in connection with some of their older members, who are not as well off as they should be and who have pretty trying times occasionally. Therefore, I think the creation of that fund is a good thing and can be made most useful as regards men who retire from the force. I think I am safe in stating that to the committee from my personal knowledge of the situation in regard to those matters.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am quite in agreement
with what the minister has said as to the propriety and advisability of forming a fund of that kind, but I see no logical connection between that and creating it as a proportion of the fines.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Is the minister able to
say anything regarding those Royal North West Mounted Policemen who went overseas? We know they wanted to be the first to go; but they could not go for a while until they got the necessary permission, and they had to take less pay over there and were not on the same rate of pay at that time as the members of our Canadian Expeditionary Force. I happened to come down on the train and saw a tourist car full of them. They were discussing that point. They were anxious to come back to Canada when the war was over, if they were alive. But under the peculiar regulations then of the North West Mounted Police Force, they could not draw anything whatever by virtue of their having to go over, and they had to take less by serving in the British army. They hoped that some provision might be made by which the difference in their pay would go on, so that when they came back, they would have some little stake. Is the minister able to say that proportion of those men who served overseas have returned? They were the very best type of men, and it would be a good thing for Canada to get them back. A fund of this nature would be a benefit also. While I am on my feet, I might say, as regards the objection of my hon. friend (Mr. Euler) to any portion of the fines going to that fund, that there are many statutes, in which there are what are called Quitam penalties, and under the statute which is sometimes provincial, sometimes Dominion, half of the penalty goes to the man who lays the information. Many an officer, many a civilian, knows of these penalties and starts proceedings in order to get half of the penalty. We cannot deal with that question here except in the way in which this Bill proposes to deal with it, that is to say, that that half

which ordinarily goes to the North West Mounted Police as the informants does not go to them-if it is an Irishism to say that-and to see that at the same time they get a benefit out of it. That is the way in which I understand it.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: If the proposed change in the law is going to change the direction in which the moiety of fine is to go, why is it not just as possible to wipe it out altogether? We are making the law; we can make it to suit ourselves.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Sometimes a province
makes the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I am not able to give my hon. friend (Mr. Keefer) the information at the present time. As I did not know that this matter was coming up, I have not the information at hand. I will make inquiry and when we are on the mounted police Estimates, I will give the hon. member information for which he asks.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
This measure is a good one and should be supported. I think it is better for the moiety of the fine to go into a fund than to an individual, not because I think there is any danger, as I heard whispered around me, that members of the police force would be too eager to obtain a conviction for the sake of what was in it. I do not believe there is any danger of that. As the hon member for Port Arthur and Kenora (Mr. Keefer) has stated, there are certain laws with statutory fees which must be collected. The opportunity may come to one member of the force very often, to another very seldom. A man who executes a warrant or has charge of a case, on account of holding a position on a detachment or where there is a good deal of work to do, may have a better time than another man who may work harder, and may get all the opportunity of obtaining this money. Therefore, he may get a great Meal more than his share, while the other man gets less. An old practice in connection with this fund was that furnishings, reading rooms, places of amusement and so on came out of the " fine " fund or " recreation " fund, but at that time it was chiefly derived from fines imposed on members themselves for misdemeanors. In the case the minister mentioned, the fund might be of great assistance to veterans or others who were in need of help, and this would be a good way of disposing of the fund. I know there are old pensioners of the police force who are not receiving anything like pensions our soldiers who served in the late

war are getting. Some of them receive as little as twenty cents a day, which was the pension settled upon them at the time, and they are to-day objects of charity. If a fund could be carried in any way, it would be of great assistance to them, and they are in need of it. The best way to distribute this money is to put it into a fund as outlined by the minister, so that it could be distributed equally Or used for the benefit of somebody who was really in need of it.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The original Act is Chapter 91 of the Revised Statutes. The amendment is marked 21 A. I do not see any connection between this amendment and section 21 of chapter 91, which provides for the salaries of the different officials. The Commissioner of Police gets $3,000 and it goes on with a list of salaries and other allowances. These deal immediately with penalties. I never had occasion to read the Act, and I do not know what the provisions of the old Act are in respect to the disposition of fines of this kind, but if the old legislation is to disappear, would it not be better to strike out the old provision and substitute the new one for it, than to have that old provision continued in the law, when notwithstanding that, something else will govern? If a person picks up the revised statute and finds a certain provision in it he is apt to follow that; the magistrate and others think that is the law; they may never come across this amendment, which says that notwithstanding anything else contained in the law its provisions must govern. I think it Would be better to have the law in one statute, if possible.
I had always understood that the fines or penalties were dealt with by the court, and that the magistrate who imposed the fine would order what was to become of the money. That is the rule, but this seems to leave it to the disposition of the minister at some later stage. I am looking for information; I do not know who is to settle the division of the money unless the court does. This seems to leave it open to some other authority who is not defined by this amendment. If the minister has a reasonable explanation of this, I have nothing more to say.	|

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I thoroughly agree with what the hon. gentleman has stated, but to follow his suggestion would mean an amendment to at least four statutes. The Mounted Police Act does not deal with this question, but there are at least four statutes, the Inland Revenue Act, the

Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, the Indian Act, and the Customs Act, which contain provisions to the effect that any informant whether a mounted policeman or not, who gives information that leads to a conviction shall be entitled to a moiety of the fine imposed; so, to follow my hon. friend's suggestion, would mean amending these four Acts. Instead of that, this amendment simply states that notwithstanding the provisions of any Act inconsistent herewith any portion of a fine or forfeiture that is payable to a member of the force shall be paid to the minister. Let us take a concrete example. A mounted policeman lays information against some person who has infringed a provision of the Indian Act. The guilty party is convicted and fined $100. The mounted policeman who laid the information is entitled, we will say, to one-half the fine. He would receive $50. Now under the old law he would pocket that himself, but under this law he must immediately forward that $50 to the minister. If the hon. gentleman will look at the statute before him, he will see that it does not deal with this question at all.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Suppose no part of the fine was paid to the mounted policeman at all; would it not be his duty to look after the enforcement of the Act in that case?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Oh, yes.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Then why pay him a portion of the fine?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is what we are trying to remove.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: But under this amendment, though he vyill not get it himself personally, it will go into a fund for the benefit of the mounted policemen. Why should not that whole fine go into the treasury to help pay the expenses of the Mounted Police Force.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: There are some statutes in this country, which have been long in existence, in which provision is made that a portion of the penalties secured against violators of the law shall go to the informant. This relates to but a few statutes such as the minister has mentioned, the Customs Act, the Inland Revenue Act, and the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: And the Indian Act.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I have had no experience with the Indian Act, but I do say that it is impossible to secure proper enforcement of legislation of that character without providing that a portion of the penalty shall go to the informant. I am sure that has been our experience in this country. It would be utterly 10 p.m. impossible to get proper enforcement of the customs regulations, for instance, in Canada merely by giving a certain definite salary, even though it might be regarded as a very good one. It is all very well for hon. gentlemen to say that a public officer should carry out his duties for the salary he receives, but there are some statutes being constantly violated and it is very difficult to secure a conviction under them because the offences are of such a nature that it requires a great deal of time, and frequently no inconsiderable expense, for the law officer to obtain the evidence necessary to secure a conviction. Therefore, it is in this country, and I fancy in a great many other countries, that a portion of the penalty is payable to the informant or prosecutor.
I should say without having any special knowledge of the work of the mounted police, that their work relates largely to 'statutory offences of that character. I think the principle is sound that the informant or officer prosecuting should receive a portion of the penalty. The minister by this amendment proposes that that proportion of the penalty usually payable to the informant or officer shall now go into a fund. I think we must either accept the amendment or go back to the law as it was. Personally, I think the law as it now stands would be preferable to the amendment, but I do not know sufficient of the practices in the West particularly, where the mounted police operate, and therefore I decline to venture a judgment, but I say that we must either accept the amendment or the law as it now stands.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend from Victoria (Alta.) has put his finger on the real weakness. Under the law as it stands, a man who happened to be fortunately situated would have opportunities that other men did not have. Let me give an illustration. So far as the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act is concerned, I think we can all realize that the main infractions of that law take place in our large centres. If I recollect rightly, we collected last year in fines something like $18,000. I do not know what portion of these fines went to the members of the force who were responsible for bringing about the convictions, but a very large'number of these convictions were dependent on action taken by

them. Now, if there were a few of these men in Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg and Vancouver, they would reap a very large harvest out of that portion of their work.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That is
their good fortune.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: But that is the objection to the present arrangement. Take [DOT] the Customs law. Out of hundreds of men engaged in the administration of that law, there are a few located along the border who look after customs work. These few have an opportunity to make money in this way that other members of the force have not at all, and it is because of that very inequality of opportunity, for one thing, that this suggestion has come. The member for Victoria (Mr. White), who is thoroughly conversant with the situation in so far as members of the force are concerned, their location, and their opportunities in this connection, will bear me out in that regard.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Where a case is brought against a defendant and it falls to the ground, it seems to me that the complainant, unless he has acted on the strongest possible evidence, should be made to pay the costs. If you put a premium on the business of supplying information, I think you leave the door open to injustice to innocent parties. The complainant is certainly interested in securing convictions, and when he happens to bring an action against an entirely innocent person, if the judge is satisfied that there is no evidence, the complainant should be mulcted in costs.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. J. A. Calder (Minister of Immigration and Colonization) , the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Resolved, That it is expedient to amend the Act to provide for the Retirement of certain members of the Public Service, chapter sixty-seven of the statutes of 1920, and to provide:_
3.	That subsection two of section three of the said Act, relating to the rate of retiring allowances to officers be repealed, and that it be enacted in lieu thereof that every officer retired under the provisions of the said Act who is not less than forty-five and under sixty years of ago who has served continuously in the public service for not less than twenty years, and every officer retired under the provisions of the
[Mr. Calder. J
sa'd Act who is sixty years of age or over and who has served continuously in the public service for not less than ten years, in addition to the payments authorized by subsection one of the said section, shall receive an annual retiring allowance payable to him during his life, equal to one-sixtieth of his average salary for the last three years during which he was in the public service for each year of his service, but not exceeding in' all thirty-sixtieths of such average salary;
2.	That subsection five of the said section three, relating to the computation of average salary, be amended by striking out the words "average annual" in the first line thereof:
3.	That the two preceding resolutions shalf be deemed to have come into operation on the first day of July, 1920;
4.	That section four of the said Act, relating to payment of expenses, be repealed, and that it be enacted in lieu thereof that any moneys payable under the provisions of the said Act to any officer retired under its provisions shall be paid out of any unappropriated moneys in the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
5.	That the time of operation of the Act be extended to the first day of July, 1922.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I note that this
resolution is completed by Resolution No. 32 on page 8 of the Order Paper respecting certain members of the public service, which is as follows:
Resolved, That the Resolutions of March 18 relating to amendments proposed to be made to the Act to provide for the Retirement of certain Members of the Public Service, chapter sixty-seven of the statutes of 1920, be amended by adding thereto the following Resolutions:-
1.	That paragraph (b) of section one of the said Act be repealed and in lieu thereof it be enacted that "officer" shall mean any officer, clerk or employee who is employed in the public service and who received a stated annual salary, and any officer, clerk or employee in the said service who is continuously employed but for only a portion of each year and who receives a daily or monthly rate of wage, but shall not include any person appointed for a temporary purpose or on part time.
2.	That subsection two of section three of the said Act be amended by adding thereto the following proviso:-"Provided that if the average salary of any officer retired under the Act for the last three years during which he was in the public service is less than the average salary oi such officer for the full term of his service, such latter average shall be taken as the basis upon which to compute any allowance to which such officer may be entitled under the said Act."- The Minister of Immigration and Colonization.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Perhaps the
minister will make a general statement upon the significance of these resolutions.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We might take up each
in turn. The first amendment proposed is the repeal of subsection 2, of section 3 of the Act as it stands. The proposed new subsection contains three changes, and I think I can probably best explain the matter by reading the law as it stands now. The first portion of this subsection reads:

Every officer retired under the provisions of this Act, who is not less than 45, nor more than 59 years of age.
It is proposed to change that to read:
Who is not less than 45, and under 60 years of age.
The reason for that is that under the law as it stands, if a man is not less than 45 nor more than 59, he is entitled under certain conditions to a certain retiring allowance. If he is over 60 years of age, under certain conditions he is entitled to another retiring allowance. You will note that no provision is made for a man who happens to be over 59 and under 60. It so happens there are a certain number retired who come in that class and they are simply left in the air.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: They are over fifty-nine and less than sixty.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As the Act reads it says: "If he is not less than forty-five and more than fifty-nine." Well, if he is fifty-nine then in six months he is between the two, and they could not deal with the case at all. That apparently was not the intention and the amendment is merely to make the correction and give effect to what was the evident intention of the law. So that the section, if amended in that respect, will now read:
Every officer retired under the provisions of this Act who is not less than forty-five and under sixty years of age shall receiveand so forth.
On that point will the minister tell us to how many officers this will apply, or give us the approximate number?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I doubt if there are very many. I have here a statement of all the officers who have been retired to the end of last month which I can give the committee a little later if they desire.
Are there many of them?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, I think 187 all told. Now the second change in the section is this: I had better read the section as it stands at present:
Every officer retired under the provisions of this Act who is not less than forty-five
I will put in the change.
-and under sixty years of age who has served continuously in the public service for not less than twenty years, and every officer retired under the provisions of this Act who is sixty years of age or,over and who has served continuously in the public service for not less than ten years, shall receive an annual retiring allowance payable to him during his life equal to ten-sixtieths of the average annual salary received by him during the last three years of his service, and in addition one-sixtieth for each additional year of service.
There was a very unfortunate wording of the law there as well, because it leaves a certain class of officials in this position: If a man was between the age of forty-five and sixty and served twenty years and another man was over sixty and served only	ten	years,	they	would each inthe first	instance	get	ten-sixtieths andthen	one-sixtieth	for	each additionalyear of service. Well, that was not the intention. The intention was that if a man was between the age of forty-five and sixty and had served twenty years, and another man was over sixty years of age and	had	served	at	least ten years,
each of them should receive one-sixtieth of his average salary for each year of his service. That was the intention and it was clearly explained to the House when the Bill was under discussion last year and was accepted by it. But the way the section is worded does not carry out the intent that was explained at that time and which the House accepted.
Reference is made to so many years in the public service. What is meant by "public service"?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Service in the Government.
In this Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

My reason for asking the question is that I know of a case where we took into the service of the Dominion Government a provincial official who had served many years provineially, and had been in the public service all his life. Although he had been serving the public all his life I suppose the provincial government made no provision for a pension for him covering the time he was in the provincial service. He is now pensioned off under the Dominion Statute but although he was receiving probably $2,500 salary from the Dominion he is now only in receipt of $1,000 a year or some other small amount. Some of our most efficient men in the Federal service to-day are men who have been transferred from the provincial service; some of them have become even deputy ministers. I need not mention any names, the gentlemen in question will easily be recalled by the House. They

have been brought from the province of Ontario into the public service of Canada and one of the reasons for making the transfer was doubtless the experience and efficiency which these gentlemen had acquired under the Provincial Government. If we are tied down, in awarding a pension to these gentlemen, to simply the service they have given the Federal Government they will, although they have been engaged in the public service all their lives, on retiring receive a less pension than if they had been federal officers during the whole of that time. In my opinion some thought should be given to this principle. I have in mind a case-I do not deem it advisable to mention names-of a very prominent medical health officer whose name is a household word in the province of Ontario, and who, in his early days, did much for the strengthening and the building up of the provincial health regulations. He was brought down here some years ago but has been retired on account of age and the pension which he receives is a mere pittance. In order to meet such cases as these I would ask whether the meaning of the term "public service" could not be broadened. While we do not want to pension former provincial officers unnecessarily, still when we take them into our service, especially in view of the fact that there is no provincial pension, we ought to recognize the long years they have spent in the public service. That course is followed by banks. When a new bank absorbs another bank it takes over the staff of the other institution and places them on its pension list crediting them with their term of service with the bank which has been absorbed. We might, perhaps, follow out that principle when we come to pension former provincial officers.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Such a policy will open up a fairly large door and I do not know where it might end.

I know cases of very
great hardship.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
At the same time I doubt very much if the responsibility for making provision for a civil servant who has been in the federal service but a short time, but happens to have been in the provincial service for a fairly long period, should fall upon the federal treasury. Coming back to the immediate subject under review there is a third change in that section as it stands in the Bill and it is this: Under the present law the allowance to which an officer who is retired is entitled is computed

upon the basis of the average salary received by him during the past three years. Well as it so happens we find that some of the civil servants who are eligible for pension have been on leave of absence either on part pay or no pay, and as a result of that, if their allowance is to be based on the salary which they actually received during the last three years, a very great injustice is done them. It is now proposed to change this law so as to make it conform to our superannuation law in this respect-that the computation shall be based upon the average salary authorized for the party who is being retired; the salary that he would actually be entitled to receive rather than the salary that he actually does receive. I think myself that the suggestion is a proper one. There are not very many cases of that kind but there have been a few, and the Civil Service Commission and the Auditor General have suggested that this change should be made.

I would like the minister to give us an illustration of how the changes he proposes are going to work out compared with the situation as it now stands. For instance what will be the difference between the two ages he has referred to. Suppose a man aged forty-five had been in the service for twenty years. How much would he receive under this new arrangement, how much would he receive under the statute as it now stands? Then take the case of a man of sixty and over, who has been in the service for, say, ten years or even for the same period of twenty years; how much would he receive under this new arrangement as a retiring allowance and how much would he have received under the present statute?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The purpose of this first amendment is merely to clear up errors in drafting to carry out the intent of the law as it passed the House last session. There is no difference in the amounts that will be received, except in one instance. Under the law as it stands, if a man is between the ages of forty-five and sixty, and has been in the service twenty years, he would get ten-sixtieths of his average salary for the last three years. On the other hand, if a man is over sixty years and has only been ten years in the service he would begin with ten-sixtieths of his average for the last three years. Then each of them would get one-sixtieth of his average salary for each additional year of service. As I explained, it was never intended when the Bill was under discussion last year that the law should operate that way. It was merely

an error in the drafting. It was intended that in the case of the man under sixty years of age who has served for twenty years, and of the other man over that age who has served ten years, each of them shall receive one-sixtieth of his average salary for the last three years for each year of service. The section is amended merely for the purpose of carrying out what was intended in the legislation passed last session.

It is simply interpreting
last year's legislation.

The results would be
the same as intended last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

My recollection is that last year the hon. gentleman presented this as a temporary measure, and I suppose he is still adhering to that view? He is not treating this as a permanent system equivalent to our old Superannuation Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.

Of course, the general'
question remains.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
We had that Superannuation Act down to the year 1897 or 1898-

Then the Government
of that day adopted the policy under which old officials were continued under the superannuation law, but all officials appointed after that time were looked after by a retirement fund, or in other words a compulsory savings fund for the benefit of those officials. As I have already said, I think that policy was a mistake, but in the execution of that policy a large number of officials appointed since 1897, and not on the superannuation list at all, will of course be included in this Bill if they fall within its provisions?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If they retire.

There is still in the
mind of the Government an intention to create a general superannuation Act of a permanent character, or is this regarded as a permanent Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.
This is to meet a temporary condition?	,

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is all.

One other question.
I am speaking now in regard to a case that came under my notice. It appears to be held that to enable an official to qualify under this Bill his service must be continuous?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is the condition.
The amending resolution deals with that.

That is to say, a man who had been some years in the service, for a short time was absent, and then returned to the service. Taking both his terms he is quite an old official. However, when this was brought to the notice of the department it was held that he could not be brought under the Act. Do I understand that under the amendment he would be entitled to have his two terms considered as one continuous term?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I doubt very much if
the amendment meets that case. In so far* as the general question is concerned, it is merely proposed to continue for one year more the Bill that was passed last session, in the hope that a regular superannuation Bill will be brought down that will deal with the entire service for years to come and will be a permanent measure. Personally, I would like very much if a Bill of that nature could have been brought down this session; I am very much in favour of it. I think if cases of the kind which my hon. friend has just mentioned are deserving, we will be able to make an amendment to cover them as well.
To this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

What is the position
of an official who does not avail himself of this Bill within the year, or within the second year as it is now to be? He will be deprived of any privilege unless we have a general superannuation bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Or unless Parliament
extends this for still another year.

The official whom I had in mind occupies a prominent position, and he put his case to me in this way: I can avail myself of this Bill, but I do not want to retire, for I am blessed with health and strength, yet I do not want to be deprived of the benefits of this Bill later. I told him that in my opinion cases of that kind would be numerous and that probably further legislation would be passed to deal with them. He said: I am strong and healthy, but if I do not resign now I will be out in the cold next year.

He could
not resign now and take his pension unless he was unable to properly discharge his duties.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: These are all compulsory retirements.
After a man reaches a certain age he can very easily make a claim to retire.
But the retirements are compulsory.

I hope when my hon. friend brings down his superannuation Bill he will be as careful as possible of the public interest. According to the Auditor General's report, during the last fiscal year we paid out something over $26,000,000 for pensions. I do not know what 'proportion of that amount is for military pensions, and I would like to have some information on the point. I trust the minister will take care of the public interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It will not be done this year.

There
is really no good reason why men in the public service should be treated any differently from men who are struggling along in private service. If we are going to provide old age pensions for people in the service, it would be logical for us to also provide similarly for people outside. Many of the men who are paying pensions to these civil servants are themselves poor. That, of course, is a very large question and one which under the present circumstances we may not be able to deal with. My object in speaking about it at all is to ask the minister to be cautious about this matter and not to increase our burdens in that direction any greater than they are at present. Would the minister tell us how many pensioners we have now in the pay of the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Do you mean under this law?

Well,
altogether, exclusive of military pensions.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am not in a position to give that information offhand by any means. I understand that under the Superannuation Act passed many years ago the moneys paid in by the civil servants themselves take care of whatever moneys are paid out to them. I am not in a position to give information as to the number of
[Mr. Fielding.!
pensioners there are as the result of our military operations and in connection with the police force. I have not the details here.

I am
concerned more with the civil than with the military end of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Under the Act passed last session there have been retired, to date, some 187 officials, of an average age of 71.64 years. The average length of service of the 187 was 23.65 years. Both the departments concerned and the Civil Service Commission, so far as I know, have been handling very carefully the administration of this law. I do not know of one instance in which there has been what you might call abuse.
What was the total amount involved in the retirement of the 187?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The average salary of
the 187 retired was $1,634.96, of the 187 retired, 128 receive annual allowance, the average allowance received being $620.23. I have not the total amount involved, but it can be easily figured out. I have not the figures of the number who were retired simply on gratuity, and the amount of the gratuity, but they can be ascertained.

While I am under the impression that the Act passed last session has been well administered, it has come to my knowledge that in a few cases the retirement of officials under this law has been carried out rather hastily. I have in mind a gentleman who was in the Customs Department in Montreal. He was appointed a short time ago, having been associated previously with a reputable firm of manufacturers in that city. Suddenly last winter he was informed that after a certain day his services would no longer be required. His superior officers appeared to be surprised at the decision arrived at in Ottawa. The man had reached the age of 69 or 70, but was perfectly strong and healthy and quite willing to continue his work. He remonstrated to his superior officers, but without avail. He had been receiving a salary of $1,500 or $1,600. When a man is able to perform his duties properly, is in good health and is willing to work, he should not, I submit, be dismissed -or pensioned; but if you are given a small gratuity and informed that your services are no longer required, I call that dismissal, pure and simple. I can give the particulars to my hon. friend if he requires

them. There is another point which I should like to bring up. When the amendments to the Civil Service Act and the proposal for the Civil Service reclassification were under consideration, I directed the attention of the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) who was in charge of the legislation, to the fact that a few old gentlemen who had been superannuated many years ago jvere suffering from the high cost of living, and I made a plea in their favour. I contended that if civil servants were entitled to higher pay and even to a bonus, old men who had served for a long time and were now superannuated were entitled to a proportionate allowance on account of the high cost of living. I rememeber that the junior member for Halifax promised me that he would consider those cases. There are very few of these gentlemen, but they are numerous enough to have formed themselves into an association, and they are writing letters to members and interviewing them and pleading their case as earnestly as possible. I would like to know from the minister if that matter has been considered by the Government? I see that the Minister of Trade and Commerce, with other members of the Government, lately received a delegation from the Civil Service. The Government had publicly announced that the Civil Service bonus would be cut by twenty-five per cent, but since hearing the delegation they have receded from that position and are now considering the advisability of maintaining the whole bonus. I have nothing to say in the matter, but it might be an occasion for the Government to consider wdiether or not old faithful servants who have been superannuated and are suffering just as much as civil servants from the high cost of living, should receive bonus or be considered when any adjustments are being made in that connection.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I should be very glad
if the hon. member would let me have the particulars with regard to the case he mentions.

I will give the name at once. He is Mr. Barsalou of the well known family of Barsalou of Montreal. His family were connected with Benning & Barsalou, an old auctioneering firm of that city. He was himself a manufacturer, and was indeed greatly shocked when he heard that he was to be retired upon receipt of a lump sum gratuity, when he was perfectly well able to perform his duties. Mr. Chairman, we have in this 158
House men who are over seventy. I claim that the men over seventy in this House are perhaps doing better service than the young men. Who would think, looking around us this evening, of suggesting for one moment that men in this House who have reached the age of seventy are not able to perform their duties as representatives of the people? In the Civil Service, I grant that there are men under seventy, who are disabled, who are not in a position to perform their duties; but when a man is seventy and is strong and healthy and willing to work, why should he be stranded in such a way?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Dealing with this question, I should like to point out that, under the Bill of last session, we took care of just such cases as the hon. gentleman refers to. It will be remembered that this section was inserted in the Bill after it came before the House.
