When it is decided to retire any person under the provisions of this Act notice in writing thereof giving the reasons for such retirement shall he sent to such person, and he shall have the right to appeal to the Civil Service Commission, and the Commission, _after giving such person an opportunity to be heard, shall make a full report upon the matter to the Governor in Council, and the decision of the Governor in Council thereon shall be final.
Under the law the Civil Service Commission, in the case of persons over sixty-five years of age, had to obtain from each of the departments a list of all persons who, on account of advancing age or ill-health or other causes similar to that, should be retired, and if I am not mistaken, out of a total list of about 1,700, reports came from the various departments to the effect that about 600 should be retired. Notice was at once sent to those people, and somewhere in the neighbourhood of two or three hundred appeals came in, and each of those appeals is being heard and carefully considered by the commission. While it is possible that injustice may be done, that mistakes may be made, still at the same time men are not retired from the Civil Service merely by sending them a letter and telling them that we are through with them. If the case is a deserving one, if the man thinks he has good ground for appeal, that there is still work for him to do and he is giving valuable service, he has under the law full right to place his case before the commission, and I doubt very much if the commission, if the man has a good case, would recommend to the Governor in Council that he should be retired.

speakerposition: topic

speechtext:
I have
never been able to give my assent to this Bill; I have always thought it was wrong in principle, fundamentally wrong, for the [DOT] reason that it proposes to afford a pension system to certain members of the Civil Service who happen to live between 1920 and 1923. Along with the statute is the public declaration that after one year the Act expires. It is manifestly unjust and fundamentally wrong to attempt to provide pensions for members of the Civil Service who, within a given period, happen to reach a certain age or, perhaps, are not quite efficient. The most that can be said for this measure is that it is the beginning of a permanent Superannuation Act' such as we should have in this country. I should think that the minister will agree with me that this particular legislation must continue upon our statute books until it is replaced by a permanent Civil Service Superannuation Act. It would be manifestly unjust, absolutely indefensible, to decline to pension certain of those engaged in the public service in say 1925, were they disqualified for the reasons set forth in the statute under discussion, and to pension those who happen to live between 1920 and 1922.
I quite agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). There should be a permanent Superannuation Act in this country, and it was a great misfortune that the former Act was ever repealed. We are the largest employer in Canada and all employers in Canada of any substantial proportions, such as banks, railways and a great number of our larger industrial concerns, have superannuation systems. The only reason why I should give my support to this Bill at all is that it holds out some hope that this will develop into a Superannuation Act, because it never can be discontinued.

The minister states
that, in the legislation passed last session, an appeal is provided for those who are pensioned, and so long as members of the Outside Service come under the Civil Service Commission, that is somewhat of a guarantee, I must say, that they will receive justice, although, when a man is notified officially that his services will be no longer required, there is a prejudice at once created in the mind of the commission that, by his superior officers in the department, he is no more of service to the public. I have, however, certainly the

fullest confidence in the fairness of the Civil Service Commission on that appeal.
I am informed on pretty good authority that the Government intend at the present session to introduce a Bill relieving the Civil Service Commission of what we call the Outside Service. Supposing a member of the Outside Service is thus relieved of his work and pensioned by virtue of this legislation, which is only amending past legislation, there will no longer be an appeal for that member of the Outside Service because the Outside Service will not come under the Civil Service Commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Even if what the hon. member says might happen, did happen, I doubt very much-
Will my hon. friend deny that it is going to happen?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am neither denying or affirming at the present time. That is a question of policy. I have under my hand a list of all retirements down to the end of March of this year, and the name which the hon. gentleman has given to the cou-mittee, so far as I can see, is not included in this list. It is quite possible that he has received notice of retirement. He has a right of appeal and he probably has lodged an appeal. That appeal may be before the commission at the present time.
What proportion of those who have been notified have been retired? I have looked over the papers, but I forget. I think it is about twenty per cent.
I agree with the remarks-
I should like to have an answer to my question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Mr. Lalor has the floor. He has been attempting to get the floor for the last half hour.

I want to agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Maison-neuve (Mr. Lemieux). I know that in my section of the country custom house officers, for instance, are being retired pretty generally, whether they want to be retired or not. I know of cases of men who are fully competent to discharge their duties and fully able to carry on who are being retired under this Act; if they do not retire by the first of June they will lose their superannuation. These men have to be replaced, and I think it is a great hardship that a man who is fully able to discharge his duties should be retired in this way. Furthermore, it is only adding to the ex-

penses of the country to retire men who are fully competent and to replace them with others.
But the Act has not only been applied to the Customs Department. It operates also in the Public Works Department. In my section of the country, I understand that the Superintendent of the Welland canal, who is fully able to discharge his duties, and is a splendid officer, respected and esteemed by everybody-he was appointed by the late government, I think- is to be retired. He is a man of about sixty-five and, I repeat, a splendid officer. Another man will have to be appointed in his place. That is another case of great hardship, and it is only adding further expense to the country. I understand that even carpenters and labouring men who have been working on the canal for years, and who are still able-bodied men are to be retired under this Act and their places filled by other men. It is simply adding to the expenses of the country without giving us any more efficient service than we have now. I think we are going altogether too far in this respect. Whether it is the commission or the Government who is responsible I do not know, but I think it is a mistake, and I think the Government or the commission should very seriously consider before they retire men under this Act who are perfectly competent to perform their duties. The Act is being applied altogether too widely.

I am inclined to concur in the observations of my hon. friend who has just spoken, because it came under my notice last year in my own province that a large number of persons received notice that they were to be pensioned from the service under this Act. I know that in very many cases there was absolutely no justification for it whatever, because these men were neither old nor inefficient. I only mention this to express the hope to the minister that he will take special care to see that the Act is not abused. This Act was orignally brought forward for the purpose of securing the discharge from the public service of certain old and inefficient people in the service here at Ottawa. It was never intended that the Act should have the wide application which some persons in the service attempted to give to it last year. I do hope, therefore, that the minister will take care to see that the Act is not abused, and that it is not applied to cases to which it was never intended to be applied. I want to call the
158&
minister's attention also to this: The last clause of the Act provides that "No person shall be retired under the provisions of this Act after the 1st day of July, 1921." Is it proposed to amend that?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The existing law will be extended for one year.
Until 1922?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

I cannot help but remark that that is very, very objectionable. It should have a more stable tenure than that, because notwithstanding Acts of Parliament and members of Parliament, people will persist in growing old and inefficient in the public service. If such cases exist to-day, the reasons for legislation of this kind will exist just as strongly every year in the future. The very fact that the period is so limited
11 p.m. brings about the condition which my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's thought did exist, namely, that people can apply for superannuation under this Act, and that is one way in which the Act can be abused. Some person nearing the age limit, and whose career in the public service is likely soon to end, can easily have a recommendation from his superior officer that he is growing too old for the public service and should be retired.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I doubt whether the
allowances are large enough to hold out that inducement.

There is the further fact that in 1917, 1918, 1919 and 1920 persons were forced out of the public service without receiving one cent of pension. In 1920 and 1921 a few people went out with $300 or $400 or $500 or $600 for the rest of their lives.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Old civil servants.

Yes, but
there were a lot of old civil servants let out between 1897 and 1920 who did not receive any pension. The point I want to make is, that those who go out under this Act are receiving a privilege which hundreds, and perhaps thousands, would like to have shared in during all the years between 1897 and 1920. Therefore, I say this Act was only intended to be applied in a limited sense. Some departments made a mistake in putting this Act into operation last year. They sent out hundreds of letters that never should have gone out. There should not be 187 people

to be retired under this Act in all Canada. I have personal knowledge, as my hon. friend knows, of the steps leading up to this legislation which went through last year, and I know it was only intended to take care of aggravated cases, cases where undeniably men were absolutely unfitted for further service either by age or by indisputable inefficiency. It would be unfair, unjust to the great numbers who have gone out in previous years, and unfair to those who are to go out after 1922, to apply this Act unless we have a permanent superannuation Act to look after the future. While the Act does remain on the statute book, I say that it should be strictly interpreted and the pension given only to those who are an incumbrance to the Civil Service.

Personally, I have not the slightest objection to men applying for superannuation under this Act, but I think it is too sweeping altogether to say that they must be retired at the age of 65 whether they want to be or not. That works a great hardship.

The Act
does not say they must be retired at 65.
That is the inference that the men in the service are drawing from a reading of the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Just a word in reply to the hon. member for Halifax. I must say that I take direct issue with the view he takes on the main question. In my judgment this Act was never intended to apply only to the Inside Service at Ottawa. More than that, I think it would be very unfair and unreasonable if such were the case.
I did not say that. I said that the original purpose of the Act was to retire from the public service those who had grown inefficient, particularly those in the departments at Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Well, if the hon. gentleman takes that view, I doubt very much if he will find upon examination that there have been any abuses. I shall be only too glad to hand over to him the lists that give the names, the positions held, the length of service, and payments made either in the way of gratuity or of allowance, and I do not think he will discover any abuses along the lines he has suggested. It seems to me that if the Act is to stand at all it must be applicable not only to departments at Ottawa but to the [Mr. A. K. Maclean. I
entire service. Let me give an illustration. I will not mention names, but we had in one of the departments a gentleman who had been in the service thirty or thirty-five years in British Columbia, drawing a salary for years without doing one single tap of work. For years he did absolutely nothing and drew in the neighbourhood of $1,800 a year. This was an outside man attached to one of the departments. I could give the case of another man in Manitoba who drew some $1,800 a year, year after year, for several years and never did one single stroke of work.
There is a way of dealing with cases like that; abolish the office and let the man go out.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
You will find, all through the service, both inside and outside, men who have grown old in the employ of the Government. Take the first example I gave

as I said, I will mention no names. This man had been long years in the service and had reached the age of 79, 80, or 81. He was probably living on the salary he drew, with nothing else to depend upon. Now, it is very easy to say, retire him. As a matter of fact, that man had been carried along year after year simply because of his circumstances.
When he is pensioned, do you intend to replace him with another civil servant?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, he will not be replaced, nor will the second man of whom I have spoken. And there are many similar cases in which the person retired will not be replaced. As my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean), well understands-and this is something for which no government is reponsible-when men get into the service the tendency always has been for them to remain in it. They grow old in the service, and once they pass the age of 60, 65, 69 or 70, no Government in the world is going to turn them out unless they have something to live upon. No government has done this in the past, and no government will do it in the future.
They did.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
They do not, and the object of the Bill of last year was to provide at least something upon which these people could live. Many of them were not required, yet every one hesitated to retire them. That aplied, not only to the inside service, but to every branch of the outside service as well, and so long as the Act

stands it should be made applicable to all parts of the service.
The hon. member forgets that there was a Government that turned out about 25,000 men at one time for political reasons;-no, I think 12,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I was referring to people over the ages of 65, 68, 70 and upwards.

But I am referring to men who were not over age at all; I am talking about people who attended to their duties and who had committed no fault except what was reported by that particular Government as a political offence.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I suppose all parties and Governments have done that in the past.
A great many were turned out and twice the number appointed instead.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Very bad.

Now, the minister has not replied to the charge made by the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), and the member for Halifax. If it is true that this Government is retiring men who should not be retired, and replacing them with other men, thus putting a double burden on the country in the way of pensions to men improperly retired and salaries to new men, this is a very grave abuse that should not be tolerated. The minister ought to give the facts of the matter. If he has 182 officers whom he wishes now to retire it is important that the committee should know who they are, what their names are, where they live, the work they are doing, and the reasons for their retirement. I must confess I have lost confidence in the administration of the Civil Service to a large extent under the present Government, and I want to know before I assent to any new legislation, or sanction any new vote of money for these services, what the Government are doing in that respect. If it is true that they are retiring men who are well able to do their work, as in the case mentioned by the member for Maisonneuve, it is of course unpardonable at the present time, when money is so precious and when the debt of the country is increasing so rapidly. I do not think my hon. friend has given sufficient attention to that phase of the question. The hon. member for Halifax is well posted in these matters, every one accepts his word, which is his bond and when he makes a statement that he is aware of numerous cases of that description that have arisen during the
past year, I think it calls for something more than the minister has given in 'reply.

May I correct my hon. friend?
Mr. CALDER. Hear, hear.

What I
did say was that it had come to my attention during the year that a large number of persons had been notified that they were to be retired, as the statute requires, and who to my certain knowledge might very well continue. I did not say whether they were in the end discharged or not. The minister has absolutely failed to catch the purport of my remarks, or else I neglected to make myself clear to him. The Act is on the statute book, and I am glad that it is there, to be applied in some cases at least. The point I wish to impress on the committee is that that legislation was intended to take care only of those in the Civil Service who obviously were unfitted physically, mentally, and otherwise for further service.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And also, if there was no further employment for them; there were the two reasons stated in the statute.

Yes. Now, possibly those who were old should be entitled to superannuation, but not if they were young people. The weakness of the Act is that it gives preferential treatment to those who just happened to be retired from office in 1920 and 1921, and I do hope that before very long we shall have a superannuation Act. So that the fewer that are retired at this time under this Bill, the less trouble there will be when that Act is introduced. If we introduced a general superannuation Act to-morrow these people who were retired in 1921 would be coming forward asking for the same superannuation as they would have received had they waited until the enactment of the permanent Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The member for Beauce (Mr. Beland), asked a question some time ago as to the proportion of those over 65 years of age who had been retired. There were 1,599 reported by all the departments as being in the service and over 65 years of age, and of that number the departments recommended 650 for retirement.

Does that necessarily
mean that they were retired?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No. Of this number 72 were* contributors to the superannuation fund. Of the 650 recommended for retirement 211 appealed; I am giving the figures to December 31. I have a statement of those retired since then, but it has not been worked out fully. Of the 211 appeals, there were 92 actual retirements at the end of December or 92 actual retirements out of some 650 recommended for retirement.
What conclusion does the minister draw from that?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Just one moment. Since then, that is during the months of January, February and March of this year, there have been some 95 retired in addition making a total of 187 retirements since the Act came into force. Now, as I stated, there were in the entire service 1,600 in round numbers over the age of sixty-five. Of these 650 have been recommended for retirement and down to date only 187 have been retired. Yet the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) speaks of the wide abuse of the administration of the law. He spoke of young men being retired. I had already pointed out to the committee that the average age of the 187 retired is no less than 71.64.
The average age?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes the average age is 71.64. Well I think hon. gentlemen will realize at once that if there were a large number among the 187 who were young men you would not have that average.
I was not talking about young men. I never used the expression all the evening until a moment ago.
How does it come that 1,600 men have been recommended for retirement?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not say that. I said there were 1,600 in the entire service over sixty-five years of age, and of these 650 were recommended for retirement.
Who by?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: By the department.
I would say to the minister that if 1,600 were recommended by some one in the department-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I repeat that I did not say that. I said there were 1,599-in round figures 1,600-in the service-over sixty-
[Mr. BSland.)
five years of age and of this number 650 had been recommended for retirement.
Who recommended the retirement of this 650.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If I remember rightly the Civil Service Commission under the law in regard to men over sixty-five years of age make their own inquiry.
The Act says:
The Civil Service Commission shall, immediately after the passing of this Act, and after consultation with the deputy heads prepare and submit to the Governor in Council a report on all officers of sixty-five years of age and over, and all such officers who are not reported to render good and efficient service-
And so on. That is, the Civil Service Commission on their own motion, must, in the first instance ascertain, after consultation with the deputy heads, the men over sixty-five years in their department who in their judgment should be retired.
That is an unfortunate provision and ought to be taken out.
Is it not a fact that these 1,599 officials were notified their services would be no longer required?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.

I have three or four cases in my county of men who were connected with different departments and occupied positions entitling them to draw the munificent salary of $100 or $150 who were last year notified that their services would no longer be required. Now these men are just as capable of doing the little work that is necessary as they formerly were.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They were simply notified by the department.
Why are they notified by the department before some inquiry is made?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They do not come under this law.
Which law do they come under?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The departmental law, which ever department it may be.

I think the member for Lunenburg is quite correct. I have had similar instances come before me in my own constituency. I do not remember how it occurred but it was a matter of administration. I am not criticising the minister for it but I think he

should take advantage of these facts because it would assist him in seeing that the Act is not abused-that is the matter that I am particularly interested in. Now I know of cases in my own province-and I called the attention of the minister to the matter by letter last year-where certain outport customs officers particularly, enjoying a salary of perhaps one or two hundred dollars a year

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They never went through.
There is no use of my hon. friend saying " no " to me when I know it was done. I do not say it was intended, I do not know who is to blame, I simply say such a thing occurred.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman
will allow me just a moment. There is nothing in the law to prevent the Minister of Customs from retiring an out-port officer in his department if he so desires.

There is
nothing in the law which enables the Minister of Customs to retire any one from the Customs Department and give him a pension. There are only two statutes under which persons can be superannuated or pensioned. One is the regular Superannuation Act which applies to those who entered the service before 1897, and the other is the Act we are now discussing. Now I want to point out to my hon. friend once more than it is a fact that many persons throughout Canada-perhaps they were among the 650-were notified that by reason of their age they were to be retired notwithstanding the fact that they were quite capable of doing the work. I submit further that if a person was in the customs service living in a country district, working perhaps only thirty days out of the year and receiving only $100 or $200 salary, he is not entitled to a pension- it was not the purpose of the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Could you give me the name of one of these men.

I cannot give my hon. friend any name now but I
wrote the minister about it during last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If I am not mistaken,
while letters of that character may have originally gone out and while certain of the departments may have thought that that class of officials came under this Retirement Act, I doubt if in one single case of the kind any person has been retired under this law on a pension.

That may be, and if the minister had been attending to what I am saying he would long ago have learned that I did not say any of) these people were actually receiving a pension. I say that during last year these letters went out to a great number of people -no doubt there were several hundreds in Canada-advising them that they were to be retired under the Act. I say it was not good administration of the Act to have these letters go out in the manner they did. I never said these persons were receiving a pension under the Act, never insinuated that at all. What I was trying to impress upon the minister was the fact that some persons in some department, or the Civil Service Commission possibly, intended originally to widen the application of the Act, and gave a wrong impression to the public and to many in the service. That is what I am trying to correct and I again express the hope that the minister will see to it so that too many people in the service will not get the impression that they are entitled to a pension under this Act. The Act was originally intended, as I have already said, to deal with exceptional cases where persons-by reason of age, inefficiency or one cause or another-were not suited to continue their work in the public service and should be retired.

While I have no
knowledge whatever of the cases referred to by the member for Halifax I think he will agree with me that if such a mistake did occur the civil servants in question should be very well satisfied now that they have not been retired. In the administration of this Act as well as the administration of all Acts' relating to the Civil Service, there will be a great deal of dissatisfaction created among civil servants. That is the effect of every Act passed which changes their status in any way. I am sure a person who gives any thought or study to the condition of the Civil Service has found this fact established: that there are in the Civil Service-and I speak now of the Inside Service; it probably applies also to the Outside Service-many employees who are not physically able to give the country full service for the salaries which they are receiving. I might say that when the committee appointed two years ago to investigate the Civil Service were holding their sittings evidence was given which proved absolutely that many men and some women were physically unfit. Now, the

Government must face the position that these people have to be dealt with in one of two ways. The first "way is to continue them in the service at their full salaries. The second way is to afford them some means of retirement as provided under this Act. I think if we look at the matter from the business point of view, leaving sentiment aside altogether, we must come to the conclusion that the only course to take is to retire these people under this Act. The member for Halifax made the statement that 187 people have been retired. I am surprised that double that number have not been dealt with. I am satisfied that the Act has been administered very leniently in that respect and that there must be still in the service many people incapable of rendering full service for the salaries which they are receiving, and whom it would be to the advantage of the country to retire under this Act.
Now, there is another class of employees not taken care of under this Act, and I think they should be. I refer to employees under forty-five years of age. I am quite sure that in the Inside Service at least there are a number of men and women under that age who are physically unfit to carry on their duties but who are drawing their salaries as if they were giving full time. I think provision should be made for those people.
With rgard to the remarks made by the hon. member for Port Arthur, I do think that when a person has been engaged in provincial government service for a number of years, and owing to the experience which he has acquired in that service he is sought by the Dominion Government, it is not going too far to recognize the years which he has given in the provincial service as public service under this Bill. I would like to see that matter taken up for consideration. No man, I take it, would be invited to leave the provincial service and enter the Dominion service unless he were thoroughly capable, and where men are recognized in that way, I think they should also be recognized when it comes to retirement.
I am glad that the Government proposes to extend this Act. I am sure it is to the advantage of the country, financially and otherwise, and of the Civil Service, because in many cases we find these old people who are incapable of attending to duties which they have been performing for many years, and they may be heads of branches or occupying other prominent positions, and their very presence in the service prevents

the promotion of younger and capable men. In that way their continuance in the service is a decided disadvantage to the country.

The minister has made
the statement that no government ever had discharged or ever would discharge an aged official without considering his ability to provide for his old age. I would call the attention of the minister to a case in point that occurred in 1920. In the month of March an employee, who had been in the service for over sixty-five years, was dismissed on a month's notice with one month's pay. I called his attention to that case when this Bill was under consideration last year, but without result. I appealed to have the Bill dated back to the end of the fiscal year so it would cover this particular case, but the minister took the ground, possibly with good reason, ' that if he acceded to my request somebody else would come along and ask that the Bill be dated still further back. But the fact remains that here is a case to which the minister's attention was called a year ago where this Government had dismissed an employee, who had given good service in several capacities for a period of sixty-five years, without any regard to his ability to provide for himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
What position did he
hold?

He was employed on the Ottawa river in several capacities-as contractor building slides and making improvements of one kind and another. I think the member for North Renfrew is fully conversant with this man's treatment at the hands of the Government. I presented his case a year ago with all the force I was capable of, and tried to appeal to the heart of the minister then in charge of the Bill, but I must confess that my best endeavours were without success.
Now, members have asked the reason why these 187 employees have been retired since this Bill came into operation. I will tell them one reason, and if they will read section 8 of the Act they will find it for themselves. That section reads:
No person shall be retired under the provisions of this Act after the first day of July 1921.
One can imagine a man over sixty-five years of age, with finances perhaps not in a good state and possibly in precarious health, backed up against a proposition of that kind. I know many men who applied for consideration under the Act, but who

if the time had been extended would have continued in the service another year, to the advantage of the country. But they were forced by the provisions of the Act to make application forthwith. I know one man who has been in the service for twenty years and never was sufficiently paid; that man was forced to take advantage of the provision of the Act. Now, I agree with the views expressed by the member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), and the member for Haldimand (Mr. Lalor) in regard to the operation of this Act. I say, as they have said, that this Act is forcing employees out of the service who are able and willing to continue. This action on the part of the Government has a tendency to increase the cost of the public service. I would ask the minister whether those who have made appplication under the provisions of this Act will be allowed to reconsider the matter and take advantage of the opportunity to remain in the service another year? It is unfair that they should have been forced to make this application; we should deal with them fairly and squarely. If we are going to extend the time for those who have not already applied, we should also give consideration to those who have already been forced to arrive at a decision. The minister has stated that there are in the service 1,599 employees over sixty-five years of age, and that the number recommended for retirement is 650. Of these 72 were contributors to the Pension Fund; 211 appeals have been registered against this arbitrary measure, and 187 have been retired. That makes a total of 1,120, so that there are still 479 men over sixty-five years of age not accounted for. Can the minister tell us anything about these men? Also, will provision be made for men who have been forced to make application for retirement under the circumstances to which I have referred? Will they be permitted to reconsider their applications and remain in the service for another year? That suggestion seems to me to be entirelv reasonable, and I hope the minister will take the same view.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: These men had the right to appeal; they made their appeal; the appeals have been decided, the retirements made and the rate of allowance fixed. I doubt very much, therefore, the advisability of opening the question up again. Personally I would not be in favour of it.

They had the right to appeal, but they had nothing to gain by
appealing; there was the provision of the Act staring them in the face. As it is proposed now to amend the Act, if appeal was allowed to these men I venture to say that in some cases they would take advantage of it and elect to remain in the service at least another year.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend is overlooking one important consideration. Under the law men are retired on account of advancing age, ill-health, lack of efficiency or lack of employment. If they appeal, the Civil Service Commission would consider the question whether these men were capable of carrying on. I can quite understand that the hon. member for Renfrew may have his own opinion as to the capability of a certain man, particularly if he is one of his constituents and as such makes certain representations to him. On the other hand, the commission must sit as a tribunal to try these facts on appeal. They listen to all that is to be said, and they come to a conclusion as to whether or not these men should be retired.

I have a case in mind, and I view it just the same as I would view any case which occurred anywhere from Halifax to Vancouver. It is that of a man who had served for twenty years and had given excellent service, one of the most capable and efficient employees of the Customs Department.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman give his name?

Well, I do not care to give the name, because I question whether he would wish to make an appeal now. But under the clause of the Act that I have quoted, if that man had failed to make application for retirement before the first of July, 1921, he would have been debarred for all time. A man of sixty-eight would weigh this situation very carefully from every point of view and he would say: Well, I will accept the retiring allowance, whereas if he had been given the option of remaining in the service another year he would certainly have done so and have given good service.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If that man made application for retirement while he was still efficient and able to carry on, well, he broke the law, that is all. This law is not intended to retire men of that class. One other point. The Civil Service Commission and the officers of the department must first decide whether those over sixty-five

years of age are able to carry on efficiently. That is a fact that must first be determined by the Civil Service Commission plus the departmental officials.

But this
man likely got a notice that he was to be retired.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Well, in that case the Civil Service Commission plus officials of the departmet had decided that on account of advanced age, ill-health, lack of efficiency, and so on, the man should be retired.

The notice that went out to the office holder was a clear intimation to him that it had been decided to retire him on account of this, that or the other cause. O'f course he had the right of appeal, and I suppose in many cases during the year, upon evidence being submitted to the commission, the appeal was allowed and the man was not removed. We can all quite understand how persons of a certain age in the public service receiving such a notice, especially those who are not conversant with the manner in which public affairs are administered, would not like to resist the notice and would allow it to go. That is the case which my hon. friend (Mr. Pedlow) has in mind. It is a great pity that the notices went out in the form in which they did. It is quite possible that mistakes might occur.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: As regards the Department of Customs and Inland Revenue, no man received a notice of his retirement unless his case was first referred to the inspector or collector of customs of the district, who was asked to report whether the man was efficient and able to carry on properly or not. After the report of the inspector or collector of customs was sent to the department, the department turned that report over to the Civil Service Commission, and then the man was notified that he would be retired on a certain date, the reasons for his retirement being given. Then the man was notified by the Civil Service Commission that he had a right to appeal from that decision. It seems to me that the man was given every opportunity of presenting his case before the commission, or of sending in a written report if he was not able to appear in person.

There seems to be a misapprehension as regards the point I have made in connection with this particular transaction. The Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue (Mr. Wigmore) has stated
[Mr. Calder. 1
that in a case of this kind an inspector would report. I want to tell the minister and this committee, without mental reservation or fear of any kind, that the inspector who reported that this man was inefficient would need,to have some report sent in regarding himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
All these cases are
reported in that way.
If the inspector reported this man as inefficient, I say that there is not a more capable and efficient man in the customs service of this country, bar none.

speechtext:
Will the hon. gentleman

speechtext:
Confidentially, so that
I may trace up his case.

The reason why this
man did not appeal is quite clear. The man is sixty-eight or sixty-nine years of age, and he was up against the possibility that, if he delayed until after July 1 of this year, he would be debarred from the provisions of this legislation. You can easily understand the reasonableness of the man's decision, that he would take no chances after July, 1921; that he was going to take advantage of the Act. If the Act had said that the final date would be July 1922 or 1923, he would have appealed, and the department would have had the services of this man for several years to come, whereas, now they are pensioning that man and putting another in his place at $1,500 or $1,800 a year, so that the country is saddled with this additional expense. It is foolish, insane, to discharge a man of this kind.

The minister (Mr. Wigmore) says that before any of these officials receive notice of retirement, the inspector or customs officer for the district has to send in a report. I do not wish to blame the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; but I know of a case in my constituency where a man in an outport district who, perhaps, did not have to do an hour's work in a day, although he did that work efficiently and well, was notified by somebody that his- services were Po longter required. speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Not under this legislation.

I do not care what legislation it was under, but these men were given notice, although they were quite capable of doing their work in their district. The Department of Customs and other departments notified these men that their services were no longer required. Men of this class who have served the public for, perhaps, 20, or 30, or 40 years, should not have received this notice. In my opinion, it is useless to argue that they had a right of appeal to the Civil Service Commission. The Civil Service Commisson is at Ottawa, and they do not know the first thing about the matter.

Such men were under the Act last year. The minister is amending it now to exclude them. That is the matter which I brought to the minister's attention last year asking him to amend the Act to exclude those men.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The class that comes under this legislation is defined under the term "officer."
"Officer" means any officer, clerk or employee who Is employed in the public service, and who receives a stated annual salary, but shall not include any person employed for a temporary purpose or on part time.
These officers are merely part-time employees. They get only a hundred or two hundred dollars a year, and it has never been considered that they come under this legislation.
That is an annual salary.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No person who is a parttime employee shall come under this Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: A number of these men ' who have been performing duties as outport officers, and receiving fifty dollars a hundred dollars or two hundred dollars a year, have received notices and have been retired, and their positions have never been filled.
Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Because they have not been doing anything even for the small amount they are receiving.

The minister does not know his department as well as he might. The man to whom I have referred is absolutely necessary, and consequently he should not have been retired, and the fact that he has been retired necessitates the appointment of another officer. Consequently, it is useless for the minister to say that he was retired because he was not necessary. It was necessary to have an officer at this outport. I know why he was retired. He was retired because he was not on the right side of politics. He was retired because he was a Grit. That is the whole story.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not know anything about this particular case, but there are a number of cases such as I have spoken of. In this particular case, the man may not have been retired at all.
He has been retired.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Has another man been appointed?
It takes the Civil Service Commission ten years to make an appointment.

It appears that in the application of this law there have been some hardships. The minister has stated that over 1,500 men over 65 years of age

were in the service; that out of that number, 000 had received notice that they might or would be retired from the service for lack of efficiency as one of the reasons; that out of those 600, about 400 went down without any protest or appeal; that 200 appealed from the decision reached by the department and Civil Service Commission, and that 92 were retired out of this 200.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Before December 31.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And 95 since. The total number to be retired is 187 up, to the end of last month.

Let us take only the 600 the minister has referred to.
' Mr. CALDER: Out of this 600, 187 have been retired.
How does the minister explain that 600 notices were sent out, implying, of course, that there were that number in the service who were considered inefficient?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Not necessarily inefficient. They may be retired for other reasons. A man may be retired simply because there is no work for him to do; I gave two illustrations of that. He may be retired on account of his physical condition, or because he is considered inefficient on account of old age or ill health.

Does it not strike the minister that if only 187 have been retired out of the 600 to whom notices were sent, it was a hunting expedition on the part of the different departments? The departments sent out 600 notices, and some of the big game were wounded, and some killed. We can all see through that. I am sure the minister would admit that it was a hunting expedition, if he would be frank. The idea was, let us send out these 600 notices, and there will be many who will not appeal. Why? Because they will have to travel, some of them, a long distance to Ottawa and incur a big expense, perhaps hire a solicitor, and a lot of correspondence will be entailed. For these reasons many refused to appeal, although they felt in their conscience that they were still performing their duties to the satisfaction of any impartial man. I shall not press the point further, but it does seem to me that this was a hunting expedition in order that the department might retire a number of civil servants who had given very good service, and who were still in a condition to perform their duties in a satisfactory

manner. I would urge the minister, if this Bill passes, and I suppose it will, to impress upon his colleagues and the deputy heads of the departments to refrain from sending out these notices unless there is very good ground for sending them out. It is a hardship in every case where the man is still in good health and able to perform his duties.
Has the minister a copy of the notice that was sent out to these 1,599 officials?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I never sent the notices at all. The notices would go from the Commission, under the law. I have not a copy of the notice here. The notice did not go to the 1,599 officials in the service over sixty-five years of age, but only to those who were to be retired.

While I am sorry to detain the committee, it might not he objectionable if I were to call the minister's attention to section 2 of the Act, and to subsection 2 of that section. Perhaps the discrepancy which I shall point out has been responsible for these notices which have been sent out, and for the confusion which has arisen. Subsection 2 provides that the Civil Service Commission shall prepare and submit to the Governor in Council a list "of all officers who are not reported to be rendering good and efficient service for the remnuneration that is being paid them." I suppose quite a proportion of the Civil Service might possibly come within that definition. It would all depend upon the person who was rendering judgment on the capacity and efficiency of the individual. While those words are in the Act, I think I may safely say that it was never intended that this Act should be used to secure the dismissal of persons on the sole ground of inefficiency. The Act was for a bigger purpose than that.
Then subsection 2 of section 2 provides that the commission shall submit to the Governor in Council "the names of all officers who, being under sixty-five years of age, by reason of advancing age, failing health, physical disability, lack of experience, and so on." It is this subsection which really discloses the reason which the Government had in mind at the time as affording grounds for the removal of persons from the service; that is, the grounds of inefficiency were to fall specifically within that category. Section 2, which I read, is very general in its application, and I fear that it was misleading just on that

account, and has been responsible for the notices being sent out. I think the minister will agree with me that it was not the intention of this Act that people should be retired merely because they were inefficient, but there had to be a combination of circumstances, namely, age, physical incapacity, utter and obvious inefficiency, or clearly no duties to perform.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I thoroughby agree.

I would suggest to the minister that before he takes the next step with this Bill, he lay on the Table for the information of hon. members the list that he has, and also a copy of the notice that was sent out.
